topics.t: Mesopotamia: the land, its names and its sources
topics.h: Before there was a Delhi, a Rome or even a Harappa at its peak, people between two rivers in today's Iraq were already writing on clay. Welcome to Mesopotamia, where city life and writing begin.
p: Mesopotamia comes from the Greek words mesos (middle) and potamos (river): the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Most of it lies in present-day Iraq.

Names changed over time. The urbanised south was called Sumer and Akkad; after 2000 BCE, when Babylon became important, the south was called Babylonia; from about 1100 BCE, when the Assyrians set up a kingdom in the north, that region was called Assyria.

Languages: Sumerian was the first known language. Akkadian gradually replaced it after 2400 BCE, when Akkadian-speakers arrived. Aramaic trickled in from about 1400 BCE and was widely spoken after 1000 BCE.
Sources: excavated buildings, statues, ornaments, graves, tools and seals, plus thousands of written clay tablets.

Mesopotamian archaeology began in the 1840s. Europeans were drawn to it because the Old Testament of the Bible mentions it; the Book of Genesis speaks of 'Shimar' (Sumer), and a Mesopotamian flood story closely resembles the Biblical story of the Flood.

ex.q: Why did nineteenth-century Europeans fund digs in a distant desert of Iraq?
st: Recall that the Old Testament is part of the Bible, central to European Christian culture.
The Old Testament refers to Sumer and tells a story of a great flood.
Europeans hoped excavations would show that these Biblical accounts had a real historical background.
So archaeology was partly driven by the wish to 'prove' the Bible, not only by curiosity about cities.
ex.a: Because Mesopotamia appeared in the Old Testament, Europeans hoped digging there would confirm Biblical stories such as the Flood.

topics.rl: Flood stories appear across cultures. In Indian tradition, a fish warns Manu of a great flood and he survives in a boat. Comparing such myths is a classic history activity, just as Mesopotamia's own tale compares with the Bible's.

rv.summary: Mesopotamia, 'the land between the rivers' Euphrates and Tigris, mostly in Iraq, was called Sumer and Akkad, Babylonia and Assyria at different times. Europeans dug there from the 1840s because of Biblical links.
focus: Meaning of the name and regional names
remember: Babylonia after 2000 BCE; Assyria from about 1100 BCE
traps: Mesopotamia lies between the Euphrates and Tigris, not the Nile
European interest came from the Old Testament, not Iraq's location

topics.t: Geography: four zones of Mesopotamia
topics.h: How can a desert with little rain feed the world's first cities? In southern Mesopotamia, the answer flowed down from distant mountains.
p: Northeast: green, undulating plains rising to tree-covered mountains, with clear springs and enough rainfall. Agriculture began here between 7000 and 6000 BCE.
North: an upland called the steppe, where herding animals was a better living than farming. Herders and farmers exchanged produce.
East: tributaries of the Tigris were routes of communication into the mountains of Iran.

South: a desert, yet this is where the first cities and writing appeared. The Euphrates and Tigris carry fertile silt from the northern mountains; when they flood or when water is let into fields through irrigation canals, the soil becomes fertile. Despite little rain, the south's agriculture was the most productive.

Map work: Uruk, Ur and Babylon lie in the south; Mari is upstream on the Euphrates; Nineveh is in the north on the Tigris. Remember: fertility alone did not create cities; trade, organisation, writing and leadership also mattered.

ex.q: Southern Mesopotamia had very little rainfall. Explain how it still had the region's most productive farming.
st: Both rivers start in the northern mountains and carry fertile silt.
In flood, they spread water and silt over the land; channels also branched off the Euphrates.
People dug irrigation canals to take this water to their fields.
Fertile silt plus controlled water gave high yields even without much rain.
ex.a: Fertile river silt and irrigation canals from the Euphrates made the southern desert highly productive.

topics.rl: The Indo-Gangetic plain is fertile because Himalayan rivers bring silt, and canals like those in Punjab and western Uttar Pradesh spread the water. Yet big cities there grew because of trade and administration too, not soil alone.

rv.summary: Mesopotamia had four zones: a rain-fed northeast where farming began (7000–6000 BCE), a herding steppe, eastern river routes to Iran, and a southern desert made fertile by river silt and irrigation, where the first cities arose.
focus: Why the south was so productive
Fertility is not the only cause of cities
remember: Farming began 7000–6000 BCE in the northeast
Nineveh in the north on the Tigris; Uruk, Ur, Babylon in the south
traps: The south had little rain; silt and canals made it fertile
Cities also needed trade, organisation and writing

topics.t: Why cities? The significance of urbanism
topics.h: A city is not just a big village. In a village almost everyone farms; in a city a seal-carver may never touch a plough and still eat bread every day.
p: Towns and cities grow when an economy develops beyond food production: trade, manufacture and services become important, and people live close together.
Division of labour is a mark of urban life. Specialists such as seal-carvers, stone-cutters and metal-workers depend on others for raw materials and food.
This web needs social organisation: someone must arrange fuel, metal, stone and wood from far away, coordinate workers and pay them, often in rations.
As activities and transactions multiply, records must be kept, so writing becomes useful. The earliest Mesopotamian cities date to the Bronze Age, around 3000 BCE.

The Warka Head, a woman's head carved in white marble at Uruk before 3000 BCE, shows specialisation: the stone had to be brought from elsewhere, a master sculptor carved it, and the eyes and eyebrows probably held inlays of lapis lazuli (blue), shell (white) and bitumen (black).

ex.q: A stone-cutter in Uruk carves seals. List the other people his work depends on.
st: He needs stone, which is not found locally, so traders must bring it.
He needs bronze tools, so metal-workers and metal traders are involved.
He does not grow food, so farmers, and someone organising rations, must feed him.
His orders and payments may be recorded by scribes.
ex.a: Traders, metal-workers, farmers, organisers of rations and record-keepers: urban specialists depend on a whole network.

topics.rl: A Bengaluru software engineer depends on farmers in Karnataka, truckers on the highways, Indian Railways freight and bank records. Division of labour and record-keeping still define city life.

rv.summary: Cities grow when trade, manufacture and services develop. Division of labour makes specialists depend on others, which needs social organisation and record-keeping; the first cities date to about 3000 BCE.
remember: Warka Head: white marble from Uruk; inlays of lapis lazuli, shell, bitumen
traps: Division of labour, not the date, explains why specialists need not farm
The Warka Head is marble, not clay or bronze

topics.t: Metals, timber and stone: moving goods into cities
topics.h: Southern Mesopotamia had grain and dates in plenty, but try finding a good stone for a seal or a log strong enough for a cart wheel there. Cities had to import almost everything hard.
p: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, made tools for carving, building and crafts. Making it needed imported metal and charcoal for fuel.

The south lacked metal, good stone and strong timber; date-palm and poplar wood were not good for cart wheels or boats. Wood, copper, tin, silver, gold, shell and stone came from Turkey, Iran or across the Gulf.
Mesopotamia paid with its abundant textiles and agricultural produce.
Regular exchange needed social organisation: someone had to arrange foreign expeditions and the exchange of goods.
Water transport was the cheapest way to move bulk goods: boats and barges on rivers and canals. The Euphrates was called a 'world route' in old times.

ex.q: Could Mesopotamian city life have flourished without metals? Argue it out.
st: Without bronze, cutting stone, carving seals and many crafts would be very slow.
Metals had to be imported, which pushed people to organise trade and keep records.
Stone tools could do some jobs, so simple life was possible.
But the dense web of specialists and trade that made cities would have been much weaker.
ex.a: Limited city life might have been possible, but bronze tools and the trade needed to get metal were central to Mesopotamia's urban economy.

topics.rl: India imports crude oil and pays with exports like textiles, medicines and software services. Like Mesopotamia, a resource gap drives organised trade, and bulk cargo still moves cheapest by water, through ports like Mundra and Visakhapatnam.

rv.summary: The south lacked metal, stone and good timber, so it imported them from Turkey, Iran and across the Gulf, paying with textiles and farm produce. Bronze (copper + tin) was vital, and boats were the cheapest transport.
traps: Cities were not self-sufficient in metal or timber
Copper + zinc is brass, not bronze

topics.t: The development of writing
topics.h: The world's oldest 'documents' are not poems or prayers. They are shopping lists: oxen, fish and loaves of bread counted for the temples of Uruk.
p: Writing is a system in which spoken sounds are represented by visible signs.

The first Mesopotamian tablets, written around 3200 BCE, had picture-like signs and numbers. About 5,000 such lists record goods like oxen, fish and bread loaves brought into or given out from the temples of Uruk.
So writing began when society needed to keep records of transactions, because in city life transactions happened at different times and involved many people and goods.
By about 2600 BCE the signs became cuneiform (Latin cuneus, wedge; forma, shape) and the language was Sumerian. Cuneiform was later also used to write Akkadian.

Method: the scribe wetted clay, patted it into a tablet he could hold in one hand, and pressed wedge-shaped signs into the moist surface with the sharp end of a reed. Dried in the sun, the tablet became hard and lasting; each transaction needed a separate tablet.

ex.q: Why did writing in Mesopotamia begin with lists, not stories?
st: Temples collected and distributed large amounts of goods.
Many people were involved, at different times and places.
Memory could not track who gave or received how much.
So the first use of writing was to record quantities of goods: accounting came before literature.
ex.a: Because the urban economy needed reliable records of goods given and received; lists solved a practical problem.

topics.rl: From GST invoices to an RBI ledger, India's economy runs on records. Early Indian inscriptions too, like Ashoka's edicts, show how writing spreads power and administration.

rv.summary: Writing began around 3200 BCE in Uruk as lists of goods for temples, because city life needed records. By 2600 BCE signs became wedge-shaped cuneiform, pressed into wet clay with a reed.
focus: Cuneiform and how tablets were made
traps: Writing began with accounts, not epics
Don't swap 3200 BCE and 2600 BCE

topics.t: The system of writing and its uses
topics.h: Imagine having to learn hundreds of signs, each standing for a syllable, before you could write a single letter to your king. Mesopotamian scribes did exactly that.
p: A cuneiform sign stood for a syllable (like -put-, -la- or -in-), not for a single consonant or vowel. So a scribe had to learn hundreds of signs.
Writing was therefore a difficult, specialist skill and a great intellectual achievement: it gave a visible form to the sounds of a language.
Very few people could read and write. Scribes wrote letters and read them aloud to the king; letters to a king began with words like 'To my lord say...'.
Uses: records of trade and goods, dictionaries, giving legal validity to land transfers, recording the deeds of kings, announcing changes to customary laws, letters and literature.

The Epic of Enmerkar: Enmerkar, an early king of Uruk, wanted lapis lazuli and precious metals for a temple and sent a messenger to the distant land of Aratta. The story credits him with first putting words on clay. It links kingship, trade and writing, and shows Mesopotamians saw writing as a mark of the superiority of their urban culture.

ex.q: What does the Enmerkar story tell us about how Mesopotamians saw writing?
st: The king of Uruk needs goods from Aratta for a temple: trade.
He organises the mission: kingship.
He invents putting words on clay to send his message: writing.
So the myth ties writing to royal power and trade, and to the pride of city culture.
ex.a: It shows that Mesopotamians linked writing with kings, trade and the superiority of urban life.

topics.rl: Indian scripts like Brahmi are partly syllabic: each consonant sign carries a vowel sound. That is why Devanagari learners study 'ka, kha, ga' rather than single letters, a little like cuneiform's syllables.

rv.summary: Cuneiform signs stood for syllables, so hundreds had to be learnt and few could read. Writing recorded trade, laws, land transfers and kings' deeds; the Epic of Enmerkar links writing with kingship and trade.
remember: Enmerkar of Uruk sent a messenger to Aratta for lapis lazuli and metals
traps: Signs were not single letters like an alphabet
Aratta was the distant land, not Enmerkar's city

topics.t: Temples: the first great urban institutions
topics.h: Picture a building that is a god's home, a granary, a factory, an employer and an accounts office all at once. That was a Mesopotamian temple.
p: From about 5000 BCE, settlements developed in southern Mesopotamia. Some became cities of different kinds: those around temples, those that grew as centres of trade, and imperial cities.

The earliest known temple was a small shrine of unbaked bricks. Temples were the residences of gods, such as the Moon God of Ur and Inanna, Goddess of Love and War. That is why early temples looked much like houses, though they had a special outer wall with regular indentations.
People brought grain, curd and fish as offerings. The god was in theory the owner of fields, fisheries and herds.

The temple became the main urban institution: it organised oil pressing, grain grinding, spinning and weaving of wool; employed merchants; and kept written records of grain, ploughs, animals, bread, beer and fish given out. Workers were paid in rations.

Thinking about causes: geography (like the lack of metal and stone, or productive farmland) gives conditions; institutions like temples, kings and division of labour help explain growth; seals and writing are tools that grew with cities.

ex.q: Why did early Mesopotamian temples look like ordinary houses?
st: Ask what a temple was believed to be.
It was the house or residence of a god.
So it was built on the plan of a house, with rooms around a space.
A special outer wall with indentations marked it out from ordinary buildings.
ex.a: Because a temple was thought of as the home of a god, it was built like a house, but with a distinctive indented outer wall.

topics.rl: Big Indian temples like Tirupati or Jagannath at Puri run kitchens, employ staff, manage land and keep accounts. Mesopotamian temples show how a sacred centre can also be an economic hub.

rv.summary: Temples, first small shrines of unbaked brick built as gods' houses, became the main urban institution, organising production, paying workers in rations and keeping written records.
remember: Settlements in the south from ~5000 BCE
Inanna: Goddess of Love and War; Moon God of Ur
traps: The earliest temple was not a stone pyramid
Lack of metal is a geographical condition, not an institution

topics.t: Kings, Uruk's growth, new technology and seals
topics.h: Uruk grew so big that around 3000 BCE it covered about 250 hectares: twice the size Mohenjodaro would later reach. War, kings and new technology drove this growth.
p: Frequent wars over land and water made war leaders powerful. Victorious chiefs shared booty, took prisoners as guards or servants and made offerings to the gods. In time they became kings.

Kings increasingly organised the community. War captives and local people were made to work for the temple or the ruler: compulsory labour instead of agricultural tax. Ration lists record grain given to workers.

Uruk grew to about 250 hectares around 3000 BCE (and later larger, up to about 400 hectares) and had a defensive wall from early on. Many nearby villages were deserted as people moved to the city, probably for safety in wartime.

Technology around Uruk: bronze tools for crafts; brick columns; hundreds of people making and baking clay cones pushed into temple walls and painted to make mosaics; sculpture in imported stone; and the potter's wheel, which let a workshop mass-produce similar pots. Sculpture also records early rulers: a basalt stele from Uruk (c. 3000 BCE) shows a ruler hunting lions, one of the earliest images of a Mesopotamian king.

The cylinder seal was a stone cylinder, pierced down the centre, fitted with a stick and rolled over wet clay to leave a continuous picture. Carved by skilled craftsmen, it sometimes carried the owner's name, god and rank. Rolled over clay sealing a cloth bundle, jar or tablet, it guaranteed authenticity. Kings were behind institutions like defensive walls, compulsory labour and large trade missions.

ex.q: Give two pieces of evidence that kings could command labour in Uruk.
st: Look for big projects: Uruk's defensive wall needed huge labour.
Clay cones for temple mosaics were made and baked by hundreds of people.
Ration lists show workers being given grain by an authority.
These show compulsory, organised labour directed by rulers and temples.
ex.a: The huge defensive wall and mosaic cone production, together with ration lists, show that rulers commanded large-scale labour.

topics.rl: A seal guaranteeing authenticity is the ancestor of the rubber stamp on an Indian government certificate or the hologram on a PAN card. Harappans, too, used seals, though theirs were flat stamp seals.

rv.summary: War leaders became kings who commanded compulsory labour. Uruk grew to about 250 hectares with a defensive wall. New technology included bronze tools, clay-cone mosaics, the potter's wheel and cylinder seals that guaranteed authenticity.
remember: Cylinder seal rolled on wet clay = authenticity
Basalt stele of a ruler hunting lions
traps: Villages were deserted for safety, not because of the potter's wheel
Seals were rolled on clay, not stamped on paper

topics.t: Life in the city: families, wealth and the houses of Ur
topics.h: In the royal tombs of Ur, excavators found gold vessels, golden daggers and harps inlaid with shell and lapis lazuli. A few streets away, ordinary families swept their rubbish into narrow lanes.
p: Society was unequal: a small elite held a large share of wealth, as shown by the royal tombs of Ur with jewellery, gold vessels, wooden musical instruments inlaid with white shell and lapis lazuli, and ceremonial gold daggers.
Legal texts suggest the nuclear family was the norm, though a married son and his family often lived with his parents. The father was the head of the family.

Marriage: a declaration of willingness, the bride's parents' consent, a gift from the groom's side, exchange of gifts and a shared meal with temple offerings at the wedding; the bride received her share of inheritance from her father. Sons inherited the father's house, herds and fields.

Ur's residential area, excavated systematically in the 1930s, had narrow winding streets that carts could not reach, irregular house plots and no town planning. There were no street drains like Mohenjodaro's; drains and clay pipes led rainwater into sumps in house courtyards, as roofs sloped inwards.

Rubbish swept into streets raised street levels, so thresholds were raised to keep mud out. Light came from doorways opening onto courtyards, giving privacy. Omens: a raised threshold brought wealth, but a door opening outwards meant a troublesome wife! Ur had a town cemetery with royal and commoner graves; some people were buried under house floors.

ex.q: Using the houses of Ur, show that Ur had no town planning. Compare it with Mohenjodaro.
st: Streets at Ur were narrow and winding, unlike planned grids.
House plots were irregular in shape.
There were no street drains; water went into courtyard sumps.
Mohenjodaro, by contrast, had planned streets and street drains.
ex.a: Winding streets, irregular plots and the absence of street drains show Ur lacked town planning, unlike Mohenjodaro.

topics.rl: Old city lanes in Varanasi or Old Delhi's mohallas also grew without a master plan, with narrow winding streets where goods often move by hand-cart rather than truck. Planned Chandigarh is the opposite, more like Mohenjodaro.

rv.summary: Ur's royal tombs show a rich elite. Families were mostly nuclear, headed by the father. Ur's residential area had winding streets, irregular plots, no street drains and courtyard-lit houses, showing no town planning.
remember: Bride got her inheritance from her father at marriage
Rainwater into courtyard sumps; no street drains
traps: Ur had no town planning, unlike Mohenjodaro
Light came from courtyards, not street windows

topics.t: Mari: herders, farmers and Amorite kings
topics.h: Herders bring flocks to a farming town. Will they fight or trade? At Mari, the answer was often both, and sometimes the herders became kings!
p: After 2000 BCE, the royal capital of Mari flourished, not on the productive southern plain but much further upstream on the Euphrates.

Farming and herding went on side by side. Herders exchanged young animals, cheese, leather and meat for grain and metal tools. But there were conflicts too: flocks might trample crops, and farmers might block herders' access to water.
Nomadic groups from the western desert filtered into the farming heartland. Some of them, such as the Akkadians, Amorites, Assyrians and Aramaeans, became ruling groups.

The kings of Mari were Amorites. Their dress differed from that of the original people, and while they respected the gods of Mesopotamia, they also raised a temple at Mari for Dagan, god of the steppe.
Mari shows that herders were not necessarily a threat to towns: they traded, settled and even ruled. Mesopotamian society was open to different peoples, and this mixing may explain its vitality.

ex.q: Explain why mobile herders were not necessarily a threat to Mesopotamian towns.
st: Herders supplied animals, cheese, leather and meat that towns needed.
They took grain and metal tools in return: a two-way exchange.
Some herder groups, like the Amorites, settled and became rulers of cities like Mari.
Amorite kings honoured local gods as well as Dagan, so cultures blended.
ex.a: Herders traded with towns, settled in them and even ruled them; exchange and mixing were as common as conflict.

topics.rl: In Rajasthan and Gujarat, Raika and Rabari herders have long grazed flocks on harvested fields, manuring the soil in exchange for grain. Herder-farmer exchange is ancient and still alive.

rv.summary: Mari, upstream on the Euphrates, flourished after 2000 BCE. Herders and farmers both traded and clashed; nomadic groups like the Amorites became rulers, and Mari's Amorite kings honoured Dagan as well as Mesopotamian gods.
remember: Nomads who ruled: Akkadians, Amorites, Assyrians, Aramaeans
traps: Herders were not always hostile to towns
Mari was not on the southern plain

topics.t: Mari: a trading hub and Zimrilim's palace
topics.h: A palace so famous that a minor king from north Syria travelled just to see it, carrying a letter of introduction. Welcome to Zimrilim's palace at Mari.
p: Mari stood on the Euphrates where boats carrying wood, copper, tin, oil, wine and other goods passed between the south and the uplands of Turkey, Syria and Lebanon.
Agents of the king boarded and inspected cargo and levied a charge of about one-tenth of the value of the goods. Trade made Mari prosperous.
Copper came from Alashiya, the island of Cyprus, famous for copper. Tin was also traded. Since bronze (copper plus tin) was the main material for tools and weapons, this trade was vital.

The palace of King Zimrilim (1810-1760 BCE) was the royal residence and a hub of administration and production, especially of precious metal ornaments. It had about 260 rooms over 2.4 hectares, a single entrance on the north, large paved courtyards, and wall paintings.

Tablets list food for the king's table: flour, bread, meat, fish, fruit, beer and wine. Studying the palace plan shows how visitors were guided from the single entrance through courtyards to audience halls.

ex.q: A boat loaded with tin worth 100 units reached Mari. Using the one-tenth charge, how much would the king's agents collect?
st: The charge was about one-tenth of the value.
One-tenth of 100 = 100 ÷ 10.
= 10 units.
ex.a: About 10 units of value.

topics.rl: Toll plazas on Indian highways and customs at ports like Nhava Sheva collect charges on goods in transit. Mari's prosperity came from sitting on a busy route, like a modern logistics hub.

rv.summary: Mari prospered by taxing boats carrying wood, copper, tin, oil and wine, charging about one-tenth of cargo value. Zimrilim's palace (1810–1760 BCE) had about 260 rooms over 2.4 hectares and one northern entrance.
remember: Palace: ~260 rooms, 2.4 hectares, single entrance on the north
traps: Not 26 or 2,600 rooms – about 260
Tin mattered because bronze needs it

topics.t: Excavating towns and cities in Mesopotamian culture
topics.h: A pig's tooth in an ancient street tells you that pigs roamed freely; a city wall in an epic tells you what people were proud of. Archaeology and literature both speak.
p: Modern archaeologists dig small areas carefully, trace wall outlines, sieve soil and collect seeds, plant fragments and bones. They can tell from debris how roofs were made and how rooms were used.

Abu Salabikh, around 2500 BCE, was a small town of about 10 hectares with fewer than 10,000 people. Plant and animal remains, such as fish bones and pig teeth found in the streets, suggest that pigs roamed freely. The dead were sometimes buried inside houses.
Mesopotamians valued city life, in which many communities and cultures lived side by side. When cities were destroyed in war, they were remembered in poetry (laments).
The Epic of Gilgamesh was written on 12 tablets. Gilgamesh ruled Uruk some time after Enmerkar. After his friend died, he searched for immortality but failed and returned to Uruk.
Walking along Uruk's wall and admiring its fired-brick foundations, Gilgamesh drew comfort from the city his people had built, not from his sons: the city was a source of pride and identity.

ex.q: What does the ending of the Epic of Gilgamesh tell us about Mesopotamian values?
st: Gilgamesh fails to become immortal.
He returns to Uruk and looks at its great wall and brick foundations.
He takes comfort in the city, not in personal fame or family line.
So the city itself was a source of pride, identity and lasting achievement.
ex.a: It shows that Mesopotamians valued their cities deeply; the city was the lasting achievement a person could take comfort in.

topics.rl: At Keeladi in Tamil Nadu and Rakhigarhi in Haryana, Indian archaeologists use careful digging, sieving and DNA or plant studies to reconstruct daily life, just as at Abu Salabikh.

rv.summary: Careful modern digs at Abu Salabikh (~10 hectares, c. 2500 BCE) reveal daily life. Mesopotamians valued cities, lamented destroyed ones, and in the 12-tablet Epic of Gilgamesh the king takes comfort in Uruk's walls.
focus: Gilgamesh and pride in the city
remember: Abu Salabikh ~10 hectares, under 10,000 people; pigs roamed
Epic of Gilgamesh: 12 tablets; Gilgamesh ruled Uruk
traps: Gilgamesh failed to find immortality
The tablet count does not explain his comfort

topics.t: The legacy of writing: maths, time and the first libraries
topics.h: Every time you check that a class lasts 60 minutes or a day has 24 hours, you are using a Mesopotamian idea.
p: Mesopotamia's greatest legacy is its scholarly tradition of time-reckoning and mathematics.
Tablets from around 1800 BCE have multiplication and division tables, square and square-root tables, and tables of compound interest. One tablet gives a value for the square root of 2.
The division of the year into 12 months, the month into 4 weeks, the day into 24 hours and the hour into 60 minutes has come down to us from the Mesopotamians.

Eclipses of the sun and moon were recorded, and the positions of stars and constellations were observed. Writing made it possible to pass on such knowledge; students in schools read and copied earlier tablets.

An early library: the Assyrian king Assurbanipal (668-627 BCE) gathered tablets at his capital, Nineveh, about 1,000 texts in all. He sent people to find old tablets; scribes copied them, and the collection was catalogued, with tablets grouped by subject.

ex.q: A Mesopotamian scholar counted time in hours of 60 minutes. How many minutes are in one day of 24 hours?
st: 1 day = 24 hours
1 hour = 60 minutes
ex.a: 1440 minutes

topics.rl: India's Jantar Mantar observatories and ISRO's eclipse predictions continue the tradition of observing the sky. Libraries like the Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Library in Patna preserve and catalogue old manuscripts, much like Assurbanipal's scribes.

rv.summary: Mesopotamia's greatest legacy is time-reckoning and mathematics: c. 1800 BCE tables, our 12-month, 24-hour, 60-minute divisions, records of eclipses, and Assurbanipal's catalogued library of about 1,000 texts at Nineveh.
remember: Maths tablets ~1800 BCE, incl. square root of 2
Assurbanipal 668–627 BCE; ~1,000 texts, grouped by subject
traps: Don't confuse Assurbanipal's dates with Zimrilim's
Don't say the week has 10 days or the day 100 hours: a month has 4 weeks and a day 24 hours

topics.t: Babylon, later conquests and the Mesopotamian timeline
topics.h: A king who dug up ruins of an older king and repaired his statue: Nabonidus of Babylon has been called an 'early archaeologist'.
p: In 625 BCE, Nabopolassar freed Babylonia from Assyrian rule. His successors expanded the kingdom and carried out great building projects at Babylon.
Babylon became a premier world city: over 850 hectares, with a triple wall, great palaces and temples, a ziggurat (stepped tower) and a processional way to the ritual centre.
Nabonidus, the last ruler of independent Babylon, was interested in the past: his men found a broken statue of Sargon, king of Akkad, which he had repaired. He is called an 'early archaeologist'.
The Achaemenids of Iran conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, and Alexander conquered it in 331 BCE. Cuneiform was deciphered by scholars in the 1850s.

Timeline: farming in the north c. 7000-6000 BCE; first Uruk tablets c. 3200 BCE; cuneiform c. 2600 BCE; Sargon of Akkad c. 2370 BCE; Mari flourishes after 2000 BCE; maths texts c. 1800 BCE; Assyrian empire 720-610 BCE; Assurbanipal 668-627 BCE.

ex.q: How many years passed between Nabopolassar freeing Babylonia (625 BCE) and its conquest by the Achaemenids (539 BCE)?
st: Both dates are BCE, so the earlier date has the larger number.
Subtract: 625 − 539.
= 86 years.
ex.a: 86 years

topics.rl: Indian kings too valued older rulers: Ashoka's pillars were later re-inscribed by others, and Firoz Shah Tughlaq moved two Ashokan pillars to Delhi. Rulers often use the past to strengthen their own image.

rv.summary: Nabopolassar freed Babylonia in 625 BCE; Babylon grew past 850 hectares with a triple wall and ziggurat. Nabonidus repaired Sargon's statue. The Achaemenids took Babylon in 539 BCE, Alexander in 331 BCE.
remember: 625 BCE Nabopolassar; 539 BCE Achaemenids; 331 BCE Alexander
traps: For BCE dates subtract smaller from larger: 539 − 331 = 208
Alexander did not conquer Babylon in 539 BCE

topics.t: Two empires and the Mediterranean world
topics.h: Imagine one government ruling Spain, Egypt, Syria and England at the same time. For centuries, Rome did exactly that, with the Mediterranean Sea at its centre.
p: Between the birth of Christ and the early seventh century, two powerful empires dominated much of Europe, North Africa and West Asia (the Middle East): the Roman Empire and the Iranian empire, ruled first by the Parthians and then by the Sasanians.
The two were neighbours and frequent rivals, separated only by a narrow strip of land running along the river Euphrates.

The Mediterranean Sea was the heart of Rome's empire. Rome controlled all the territory around it: Spain and Italy in the west, Greece and Asia Minor (Turkey), Syria and Egypt in the east, and North Africa in the south.

Map work: the northern frontier ran along two great rivers, the Rhine and the Danube; the southern frontier was set by the Sahara desert. Within this vast space lived many peoples, languages and cultures.

ex.q: Why do historians call the Roman world 'an empire across three continents'?
st: List the regions around the Mediterranean that Rome controlled.
Spain, Italy, Gaul, Greece belong to Europe.
Syria, Asia Minor and Palestine belong to Asia (West Asia).
Egypt and North Africa belong to Africa.
ex.a: Because Roman territory stretched across Europe, West Asia and North Africa, all linked by the Mediterranean.

topics.rl: The Indian Ocean linked Indian ports like Arikamedu and Muziris to the Roman world: Roman coins and amphora pieces have been found in South India, showing trade reached even beyond the empire's three continents.

rv.summary: From Christ's birth to the seventh century, the Roman and Iranian (Parthian, then Sasanian) empires dominated. Rome ruled all lands around the Mediterranean across Europe, West Asia and North Africa, bounded by the Rhine, Danube and Sahara.
remember: Separated by a strip along the Euphrates
North: Rhine and Danube; south: Sahara
traps: Iran's dynasties were Parthian then Sasanian, not Achaemenid
China was never part of Rome's empire

topics.t: Sources for Roman history
topics.h: A shopping receipt, a love letter, a broken jar and a coin: two thousand years from now, these could tell historians how you lived. That's how we know Rome too.
p: Textual sources: histories of a period written by contemporaries (often called annals because written year by year), letters, speeches, sermons and laws.
Documentary sources: mainly inscriptions (cut on stone, mostly in Greek and Latin, so many survive) and papyri.

Papyrus is a reed-like plant that grew along the Nile in Egypt; it was processed into writing material. Thousands of contracts, accounts, letters and official documents on papyrus survive from Egypt and are studied by papyrologists.

Material remains: buildings, monuments and other structures, pottery, coins, mosaics, and even whole landscapes revealed by aerial photography. Amphorae (containers) and coins tell us about trade and the money economy.
Using sources critically: senators wrote most surviving histories, so their views of emperors may be biased; combining texts, documents and material remains gives a fuller picture.

ex.q: A historian finds thousands of olive-oil containers from Spain in Rome. What can she conclude?
st: Identify the source type: material remains (amphorae).
Identify where they came from: Spain, from their shape and stamps.
Ask what the quantity suggests: large-scale, regular trade.
Conclude: Rome imported huge amounts of Spanish olive oil; the economy was well connected.
ex.a: Spanish olive oil was traded on a large scale to Rome, showing a connected, commercial Mediterranean economy.

topics.rl: Indian historians use the same mix: Ashokan inscriptions, palm-leaf manuscripts, coins of the Kushanas and Guptas, and pottery from digs like Arikamedu, where Roman amphorae were found.

rv.summary: Roman history uses texts (annals, letters, laws), documents (stone inscriptions in Greek and Latin, papyri from Egypt) and material remains (buildings, coins, amphorae, mosaics), read critically.
traps: Mosaics are material remains, not texts
Senatorial histories can be biased against emperors

topics.t: From Republic to Principate: Augustus and the Senate
topics.h: The man who ended Rome's Republic never called himself king. Augustus preferred 'first citizen', while quietly holding real power.
p: Historians divide Roman history into the early empire (from Augustus down to the main part of the third century) and the late empire (after that).

The Republic (509 BCE to 27 BCE) was a regime in which real power lay with the Senate, a body dominated by a small group of wealthy families. Offices were held by members of the wealthy and aristocratic classes.
In 27 BCE, Julius Caesar's adopted son Octavian, who took the name Augustus, overthrew the Republic. The regime he founded is called the Principate.
Augustus claimed to be only the 'leading citizen' (princeps), not an absolute ruler, out of respect for the Senate.

The Senate survived for centuries, representing the aristocracy. Most surviving Roman histories were written by senators, who judged emperors by how they treated the Senate: the worst emperors, in their view, were those hostile to the senatorial class.

ex.q: Why did Augustus call himself princeps ('first citizen') instead of king?
st: The Senate had held power under the Republic and was proud of its traditions.
Openly claiming kingship would anger the aristocracy.
Calling himself first citizen showed respect for the Senate.
Yet he held real control, especially over the army.
ex.a: To show respect for the Senate and avoid seeming like a king, while in practice holding supreme power.

topics.rl: In India's Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha, power is shared by law. Rome's Senate is a reminder that institutions can survive even when real power shifts to one person.

rv.summary: The Republic (509–27 BCE) was run by the Senate. In 27 BCE Augustus, Julius Caesar's adopted son, founded the Principate, calling himself princeps out of respect for the Senate, which survived and wrote most histories.
traps: The title reflects respect for the Senate, not his adoption
Early empire runs to the third century

topics.t: The army, the three players and succession
topics.h: In Rome, an emperor who lost the army's support could lose his throne overnight. Soldiers were the empire's backbone and its biggest danger.
p: Next to the emperor and the Senate, the army was the key institution. Unlike Iran's conscripted army, Rome had a paid professional army; soldiers served a minimum of 25 years.

The army was the largest single organised body in the empire (about 600,000 soldiers by the fourth century) and could decide the fate of emperors. Soldiers agitated for better wages and service conditions, sometimes by mutiny.
The emperor, the aristocracy (Senate) and the army were the three main 'players' in politics. An emperor's success depended on his control over the army; when armies were divided, civil war followed.
Succession was based as far as possible on family descent, natural or adoptive, and the army was strongly attached to this principle. Still, armies sometimes made emperors themselves.

ex.q: Explain why the army could decide who became emperor.
st: The army was the largest organised body in the empire.
It was a paid, professional force loyal to whoever led and paid it.
If soldiers backed a rival, the emperor had no force to resist.
So control of the army was the key to power; divided armies meant civil war.
ex.a: Because it was the largest organised force and emperors needed its loyalty; without it they could be overthrown.

topics.rl: India's armed forces stand apart from politics under the Constitution, under civilian control. Rome shows what happens when an army becomes a political player.

rv.summary: Rome had a paid professional army of about 600,000 by the fourth century, serving at least 25 years. Emperor, aristocracy and army were the three players; succession followed family descent, and divided armies meant civil war.
traps: The Roman army was paid, not conscripted
Succession was by family (natural or adoptive), not elections

topics.t: Expansion, provinces and a network of cities
topics.h: Rome governed a huge empire without a modern bureaucracy or railways. Its secret: cities and cooperative local elites.
p: Augustus inherited a vast territory, and his reign was remembered for the peace it brought after decades of civil war. Later expansion was limited: Trajan's occupation of territory across the Euphrates (113-117 CE) was fruitless and abandoned by his successors.

Integration happened through the gradual extension of direct rule. The Near East had many dependent (client) kingdoms; by the early second century those west of the Euphrates had been absorbed into Roman territory.

The empire was organised as a network of cities. The city, with its magistrates and city council, was the core unit of government; through cities the state taxed the countryside. Great urban centres included Carthage, Alexandria and Antioch.

Local upper classes collaborated with Rome in administering their areas and raising taxes. In a dramatic shift of power from Italy, provincial upper classes came to supply much of the Senate and the officer class by the second and third centuries.
The 'Roman peace' was the relative stability within the empire that let cities and trade networks flourish.

ex.q: Rome had no large modern bureaucracy. How did it collect taxes across three continents?
st: The empire was divided into provinces, each with many cities.
Each city had its own magistrates and council drawn from local elites.
These elites collected taxes from the surrounding countryside.
So Rome governed through cities and cooperative local upper classes.
ex.a: By governing through cities whose local upper classes administered their areas and collected taxes for Rome.

topics.rl: Indian districts are run through district collectors, and earlier the Mughals relied on zamindars. Large states have always depended on local intermediaries, as Rome did with city councils.

rv.summary: Augustus brought peace; Trajan's eastern conquest (113–117 CE) was abandoned. Rome absorbed client kingdoms and governed through a network of cities whose local elites collected taxes; provincials came to dominate the Senate.
focus: Cities and local elites in governance
remember: Provincial upper classes rose by the 2nd–3rd centuries
traps: Trajan's conquest across the Euphrates did not last
Rome taxed through cities, not monasteries

topics.t: The third-century crisis
topics.h: Twenty-five emperors in forty-seven years. When rulers change faster than students in a school year, you know something has gone wrong.
p: If the first and second centuries were mostly of peace, prosperity and expansion, the third century brought the first major signs of internal strain.

From the 220s, a new and more aggressive dynasty, the Sasanians, rose in Iran. Within 15 years it expanded towards the Euphrates. In a rock inscription in three languages, Shapur I claimed to have destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 and captured Antioch, the eastern capital.

Meanwhile, Germanic tribes or confederacies, notably the Alamanni, the Franks and the Goths, attacked the Rhine and Danube frontiers; from 233 to 280 there were repeated invasions along the northern frontier.
The quick succession of emperors, 25 in 47 years, shows the strain on the empire.
The economy and the army were stretched: Rome had to divert more resources to defence and abandon much territory beyond the Danube.

ex.q: Using the figure '25 emperors in 47 years', show why historians call the third century a crisis.
st: Average reign = 47 ÷ 25.
= 1.88 years, i.e. under two years each.
Short reigns meant instability and frequent power struggles.
Combined with attacks from Iran and Germanic tribes, this signals a crisis.
ex.a: Emperors lasted on average under two years, a clear sign of political instability.

topics.rl: India's political stability since 1950 under one Constitution contrasts with such rapid changes. Historians often count changes of rulers as an index of stability.

rv.summary: The third century brought crisis: the aggressive Sasanians under Shapur I attacked the east, Germanic tribes invaded the Rhine and Danube frontiers (233–280), and 25 emperors ruled in 47 years.
remember: Shapur I claimed to destroy 60,000 Romans and capture Antioch
25 emperors in 47 years ≈ under 2 years each
traps: The Mongols did not attack Rome
Pompeii (79 CE) has nothing to do with the crisis

topics.t: Family, women and marriage in the Roman world
topics.h: In Roman law, a husband and wife were not one financial unit but two. Roman women could own property in their own right, surprisingly early.
p: The nuclear family was widespread in Roman society. Adult sons did not usually live with their families, and adult brothers sharing a household was rare. Slaves were counted as part of the family (household).

By the late Republic (first century BCE), the typical form of marriage let the wife keep full rights in the property of her natal family. Her dowry went to the husband during marriage, but she remained a primary heir of her father and became an independent property owner when he died.

Roman women thus had considerable legal rights in owning and managing property. Husband and wife were two financial entities, and divorce was relatively easy: a notice of intent to dissolve by either party was enough.
Men married in their late twenties or early thirties, while women married in their late teens or early twenties, so there was an age gap. Marriages were usually arranged.
Women were often dominated by husbands; Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, recorded that his father regularly beat his mother. Fathers had wide legal power over children.

ex.q: A Roman bride brings a dowry. Who controls it during marriage and what happens to her inheritance later?
st: During marriage, the dowry goes to the husband.
She remains a primary heir of her own father.
On her father's death, she inherits and becomes an independent property owner.
So she keeps strong rights in her natal family's property.
ex.a: The husband holds the dowry during marriage, but she inherits from her father and owns property independently.

topics.rl: India's Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 gave daughters equal rights in ancestral property. Rome shows that women's property rights have a long and varied history across societies.

rv.summary: Roman families were mostly nuclear and included slaves. Wives kept rights in their natal property and divorce was easy, yet women were often dominated by husbands, and men married later than women.
remember: Husband and wife = two financial entities
traps: Legal rights did not mean freedom from male power
Men, not women, married later

topics.t: Literacy, languages and cultural diversity
topics.h: Walls of ancient Pompeii are covered with advertisements and graffiti. Ordinary people writing on city walls tells us many could read and write, at least a little.
p: Casual literacy, the ability to read and write for everyday purposes, varied greatly across the empire.

Pompeii, buried by a volcanic eruption in 79 CE, had walls covered with advertisements and graffiti, suggesting widespread casual literacy there. In Egypt, many contracts were written by professional scribes for people who could not read or write.

Cultural diversity was huge: many religious cults and local deities; and many languages, such as Aramaic in the Near East, Coptic in Egypt, Punic and Berber in North Africa, and Celtic in Spain and the northwest.

Greek dominated in the east and Latin in the west. Many local languages were mainly spoken; a Coptic translation of the Bible existed by the mid-third century, while Armenian began to be written only in the fifth century. In the west, Latin displaced written Celtic.

Thinking it through: life in a Roman town offered markets, baths, entertainment and contact with many cultures, but also inequality; village life was more local and often harsher. Historians weigh both.

ex.q: Why do historians use Pompeii's graffiti as evidence of literacy?
st: Graffiti and adverts were written on public walls.
They were meant to be read by passers-by.
Writers and readers must have had at least basic literacy.
So literacy in Pompeii was fairly widespread, though it varied elsewhere.
ex.a: Because public writing aimed at ordinary passers-by shows many people could read, at least casually.

topics.rl: India is home to 22 scheduled languages and hundreds more, with Hindi and English as official languages of the Union. Like Rome's Greek and Latin, link languages coexist with rich local ones.

rv.summary: Literacy varied: Pompeii's graffiti suggest widespread casual literacy, while Egyptians used scribes. The empire was diverse in cults and languages; Greek dominated the east and Latin the west.
remember: Coptic (Egypt), Aramaic (Near East), Punic and Berber (North Africa), Celtic (Spain, northwest)
traps: Latin was not the only language
Latin displaced written Celtic, not the reverse

topics.t: Economic expansion: amphorae, olive oil and money
topics.h: In Rome stands a hill made almost entirely of broken pots: Monte Testaccio, built from the remains of over 50 million amphorae!
p: The empire had a strong economic infrastructure: harbours, mines, quarries, brickyards, olive-oil factories and more. Wheat, wine and olive oil were traded in huge quantities, mainly from Spain, Gaul, North Africa, Egypt and, less, Italy.

Liquids were carried in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome contains the remains of over 50 million vessels. Spanish olive oil was carried in containers called Dressel 20 (after the archaeologist Heinrich Dressel); finds of them across the Mediterranean show Spanish oil dominated markets for a time, taking over from Italian producers.
Fertile regions included Campania in Italy, Sicily, Byzacium in Tunisia, Galilee and the Fayum in Egypt; some regions were famous for exceptional wine or wheat.
Not all land was settled farmland: in Numidia (modern Algeria), pastoral and semi-nomadic communities practised transhumance, moving with their flocks. Expanding Roman estates squeezed their space.

Technology and money: water-powered mills; hydraulic mining in Spanish gold and silver mines on a scale not matched until the nineteenth century; well-organised commercial and banking networks; and wide use of money (gold and silver coins).

ex.q: Archaeologists find Dressel 20 amphorae from Spain at sites all over the Mediterranean. What does this tell us?
st: Dressel 20 amphorae carried Spanish olive oil.
Their wide spread shows the oil reached many markets.
Large numbers indicate large-scale, regular trade.
So Spanish producers captured Mediterranean markets for olive oil.
ex.a: That Spanish olive oil was a mass-traded commodity that dominated Mediterranean markets for a period.

topics.rl: Indian olive oil? Not yet! But think of Kerala's spices or Assam's tea reaching global markets: specialised regions producing for distant buyers is what Roman Spain did with olive oil.

rv.summary: The Roman economy had harbours, mines and factories, mass trade in wheat, wine and oil carried in amphorae, hydraulic mining, water-mills, banking and wide use of money; Spanish olive oil in Dressel 20 jars dominated markets.
traps: Dressel is an archaeologist, not an emperor
The Principate's date does not explain the economy

topics.t: Controlling workers: slaves, freedmen and debt
topics.h: In Augustus's Italy, around 3 million of 7.5 million people were slaves. Behind Rome's grandeur lay coerced labour.
p: Slavery was deeply rooted in the Mediterranean and Near East. In Italy under Augustus there were about 3 million slaves in a population of 7.5 million. Slaves were seen as an investment, especially in Italian agriculture.

When peace in the first century reduced the flow of war captives, users of slave labour turned to slave breeding or cheaper substitutes such as wage labour, which was easier to dispense with. Free labour was used extensively in public works at Rome, since slaves had to be fed and housed all year.
Slaves and freedmen (freed slaves) were often used as business managers, and masters sometimes gave them capital to run businesses.

Agricultural writers like Columella, from southern Spain, advised close supervision: grouping workers in small gangs, and keeping twice as many tools as needed so work never stopped. Pliny the Elder condemned slave gangs as the worst method.

Coercion was harsh: chain-gangs; a law of 398 mentions branding workers so they could be recognised if they ran away. Many employers used debt contracts to keep workers under control, and peasants were often trapped in debt.

ex.q: Why might a Roman landowner prefer hired free labour to slaves for seasonal work?
st: Slaves had to be fed and housed all year, even when there was no work.
Free wage-labourers could be hired for the harvest and let go after.
When war captives became scarce, slaves grew more expensive.
So for seasonal or public works, free labour was cheaper.
ex.a: Because free labourers could be hired only when needed, while slaves had to be maintained all year.

topics.rl: Bonded labour was abolished in India by the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, and Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits forced labour. Studying Rome's debt bondage shows why such protections matter.

rv.summary: Italy had about 3 million slaves among 7.5 million people under Augustus. As war captives declined, owners bred slaves or hired free labour; workers were tightly supervised, branded and trapped by debt.
remember: Columella: small gangs, twice the tools
traps: Slavery had not disappeared under Augustus
Free labour was used because slaves cost money all year

topics.t: Social hierarchies and the gold solidus
topics.h: Some great families of Rome earned up to 4,000 pounds of gold a year from their estates, not counting the produce they ate. Meanwhile labourers worked for daily wages.
p: Tacitus described early-empire society: senators (patres); leading members of the equestrian (knight) class; the respectable section of the people attached to great houses; the unkempt lower class (plebs sordida), said to be fond of circus and theatre shows; and slaves.

In the late empire, senators and equites merged into a unified, expanded aristocracy, with many families from the provinces. Yet the purely military elites, mostly from non-aristocratic backgrounds, were often more powerful.
The 'middle' class included people in imperial service in the bureaucracy and army, plus prosperous merchants and farmers, many from the eastern provinces.

The lower classes (humiliores) included rural labourers employed on large estates, workers in industry and mining, migrant workers for harvests and construction, self-employed artisans, casual labourers in cities, and many slaves, especially in the west.

Constantine introduced the solidus, a gold coin of 4.5 grams of pure gold, minted in very large numbers. The historian Olympiodorus said many great houses of Rome earned up to 4,000 lbs of gold a year from their estates. The administration had corruption, especially in the judicial system and among greedy tax collectors.

ex.q: Arrange Tacitus's description of early Roman society from top to bottom, and say who was left out of 'citizens' altogether.
st: Top: senators.
Next: leading equestrians.
Then: respectable people attached to great houses.
Then: the unkempt lower class (plebs sordida).
Slaves were at the very bottom, outside the free population.
ex.a: Senators, equestrians, respectable people, the lower class, then slaves at the bottom.

topics.rl: Modern India measures inequality through surveys like NSSO data. Rome's Olympiodorus, writing of great estate incomes, offers a rare ancient glimpse at the very top of the wealth ladder.

rv.summary: Tacitus described senators, equestrians, respectable people, the plebs sordida and slaves. In the late empire senators and equites merged, military elites were powerful, and a middle class and the humiliores existed; Constantine's solidus held 4.5 g of gold.
remember: Olympiodorus: up to 4,000 lbs of gold a year
traps: Tax collectors were criticised as greedy, not praised
Military elites were mostly non-aristocratic

topics.t: Late Antiquity: Diocletian, Constantine and a new prosperity
topics.h: A new capital surrounded on three sides by the sea, a new gold coin and a new religion: Constantine reshaped the empire.
p: Late Antiquity is the period from the fourth to the seventh centuries, marking the final, fascinating phase of the Roman Empire's evolution and break-up, with major cultural, economic and political changes.

Diocletian (284-305) abandoned territories with little strategic or economic value, fortified the frontiers, reorganised provincial boundaries, separated civil from military functions, and gave military commanders (duces) more autonomy.

Constantine consolidated these changes. He introduced the gold solidus and built a second capital at Constantinople (on the site of Byzantium, modern Istanbul), surrounded on three sides by the sea. He converted to Christianity (312) and took the decision to make Christianity the official religion of the empire; it became the sole state religion later, under Theodosius in 380.

Monetary stability and a growing population stimulated economic growth. Archaeology shows heavy investment in rural establishments: oil presses, glass factories, screw presses and multiple water-mills, plus a revival of long-distance trade with the East.

ex.q: Why was Constantinople a good choice for a new capital?
st: It was built on the site of Byzantium, between Europe and Asia.
It was surrounded on three sides by the sea, making it easier to defend.
It lay closer to the rich eastern provinces and the Iranian frontier.
So it was strategic, defensible and central to the eastern empire.
ex.a: Its location between Europe and Asia, sea on three sides and closeness to the rich east made it strategic and defensible.

topics.rl: India too shifted capitals for strategic reasons: the British moved theirs from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911. Capitals reflect where power and security lie.

rv.summary: Late Antiquity (4th–7th centuries) saw Diocletian reorganise the empire and Constantine introduce the solidus, build Constantinople on Byzantium and convert to Christianity, with renewed economic growth.
remember: Constantine's conversion 312; Christianity sole state religion under Theodosius in 380
traps: Diocletian, not Augustus, separated civil and military functions
Growth came from money and population, not the capital's site

topics.t: Christianisation, the fall of the West and the rise of Islam
topics.h: Within a century, a world of many gods became largely Christian, the western empire broke into kingdoms, and new Arab armies changed the map of West Asia.
p: Traditional Roman religion was polytheistic: cults of Jupiter, Juno, Minerva and Mars, plus many Greek and eastern deities, and Judaism as well. Christianisation in the fourth and fifth centuries was gradual, and bishops became the most important and often very powerful figures in the Christian community.

The empire's eastern and western halves drifted apart. In the West, it fragmented politically as Germanic groups took over the major provinces and founded 'post-Roman' kingdoms: the Visigoths in Spain, the Franks in Gaul, and in Italy first the Ostrogoths and later the Lombards.
The East stayed united and prosperous. Under Justinian (527-565), it reached a high point of prosperity and imperial ambition, recapturing Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Ostrogoths.

In the seventh century, the rise of Islam and the expansion of Arab rule brought the conquest of large parts of the eastern Roman provinces and of Iran, described as one of the largest political revolutions in the ancient world.

Timeline: 27 BCE Principate; 79 CE Pompeii; 113-117 Trajan's campaign; 212 Roman citizenship extended to all free inhabitants; 284-305 Diocletian; 312 Constantine's conversion; 527-565 Justinian; seventh century: Arab conquests.

ex.q: How did Christianity and Islam change the late Roman world?
st: Christianity gradually replaced polytheistic cults; bishops gained influence.
This reshaped religious and social life in the empire.
In the seventh century, Arab armies conquered much of the eastern provinces and Iran.
So the religious and political map of the region was transformed.
ex.a: Christianity transformed religious life within the empire, and the rise of Islam brought a new political order over the east and Iran.

topics.rl: India's own history shows great religious transitions, from the spread of Buddhism under Ashoka to the coming of Islam and the Bhakti movements, studied with respect for all traditions, as we study Rome's.

rv.summary: Polytheistic Rome Christianised gradually, with powerful bishops. The West broke into Germanic kingdoms while the East prospered under Justinian, and in the seventh century Arab conquests took much of the east and Iran.
focus: Fall of the West, survival of the East
remember: Visigoths – Spain; Franks – Gaul; Ostrogoths then Lombards – Italy
traps: Christianisation was gradual, not overnight
The East, not the West, survived

topics.t: A nomadic empire? Sources and the idea of 'barbarians'
topics.h: Nomads are supposed to wander, not to build empires. Yet in the thirteenth century, herders from the Mongolian steppe built a state stretching from China to Europe.
p: 'Nomadic empire' sounds like a contradiction, since nomads are mobile and empires need settled control. The Mongols under Genghis Khan built a transcontinental empire across Asia and Europe in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

Most of our sources were written by city-based chroniclers, travellers and court historians in languages like Chinese, Persian, Arabic, Russian and Latin. Many were hostile to nomads and described them as destructive.

The word 'barbarian' comes from the Greek barbaros, meaning a non-Greek, whose speech sounded like meaningless babble to Greeks. Romans used it for Germanic tribes, Gauls and Huns; the Chinese had their own terms for steppe peoples.
Historians must read such sources critically: city-based writers often exaggerated nomads' violence and inflated casualty figures.

ex.q: Why should a historian be cautious about a chronicler's claim that a Mongol attack killed over a million people in one city?
st: Ask who wrote it: a city-based chronicler, often hostile to nomads.
Ask how the number was known: there were no census counts during sieges.
Consider purpose: dramatic figures emphasised the horror of the attack.
So the figure may be inflated, though the destruction was real.
ex.a: Because city-based writers were often biased against nomads and had no reliable way to count; such numbers may be exaggerated.

topics.rl: News reports in India sometimes give very different crowd or casualty figures for the same event. Historians, like good journalists, ask who is counting and why.

rv.summary: The Mongols under Genghis Khan built a transcontinental empire in the 13th–14th centuries, but most sources were written by hostile city-based writers, so 'barbarian' labels and huge casualty figures must be read critically.
remember: Sources in Chinese, Persian, Arabic, Russian, Latin
traps: Mongol herders did not write most sources
Don't accept or reject chronicles blindly

topics.t: Genghis Khan's mandate and the fall of Bukhara
topics.h: 'I am the punishment of God.' So, according to the chronicler Juwaini, Genghis Khan told the people of Bukhara in 1220.
p: Genghis Khan believed he had a mandate from Tengri, the Eternal Sky, to rule the world. This belief gave his conquests a sacred justification in Mongol eyes.
The Mongols' reach was immense: in 1236-1241 their armies moved through the Russian steppes into Poland and Hungary, reaching the outskirts of Vienna.

The Persian chronicler Juwaini described the capture of Bukhara in 1220. After the conquest, Genghis Khan gathered the rich residents at the festival ground and told them their great sins had brought God's punishment, in the form of himself, upon them.

Juwaini also quoted a survivor who escaped to Khurasan: 'They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed.' Imagining how a resident of Bukhara felt hearing the speech is a classic way to read such a source.
Map work: the empire stretched from China and Korea in the east through Central Asia, Iran and Iraq to the Russian steppes and Eastern Europe.

ex.q: Read Juwaini's survivor quote: 'They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed.' What does it tell us, and what should we keep in mind?
st: It describes rapid, destructive conquest: sieges, fire, killing, looting.
It comes from a victim, so it records real suffering.
Juwaini wrote as a Persian chronicler, so his framing reflects his viewpoint.
So it is powerful evidence of destruction, read with awareness of the author's perspective.
ex.a: It conveys the speed and violence of the conquest from a victim's view; historians also consider who recorded it and why.

topics.rl: India's own chroniclers, from Kalhana's Rajatarangini to Persian court histories, also mixed vivid eyewitness accounts with their own viewpoints. Reading sources critically is a core history skill.

rv.summary: Genghis Khan believed Tengri, the Eternal Sky, gave him a mandate to rule the world. Juwaini recorded the fall of Bukhara (1220), where he called himself God's punishment; by 1236–1241 Mongol armies neared Vienna.
remember: 'They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed'
traps: Juwaini, not Rashiduddin, described Bukhara
Armies reached Vienna's outskirts, not Rome or Paris

topics.t: Life on the steppe: pastoralists and hunter-gatherers
topics.h: Long, harsh winters and short, dry summers: on the Mongolian steppe, farming barely worked, so people followed their animals across the grasslands.
p: The Mongols were diverse peoples linked by language to the Tatars, Khitan and Manchus to the east and Turkic tribes to the west. Some were pastoralists on the steppes of Central Asia (modern Mongolia); others were hunter-gatherers in the Siberian forests to the north.
Pastoralists raised horses, sheep and, to a lesser extent, goats and camels. They lived in felt tents called gers and moved seasonally between winter and summer pastures.
Hunter-gatherers lived north of the pastoralists, were poorer, and lived by trading furs from animals they trapped.
The harsh climate allowed agriculture only in limited seasons, and neither economy could support large populations, so no cities arose on the steppe.

Society was organised in patrilineal lineages; richer families were larger, owned more animals and pasture, and had many followers. Alliances and confederacies formed for defence or raids but were usually small and short-lived.

ex.q: Why did no cities develop on the Mongolian steppe?
st: The climate had harsh winters and short, dry summers.
Agriculture was possible only in limited seasons.
Herding and hunting could not support large, dense populations.
So people lived in small mobile groups, not cities.
ex.a: The harsh climate limited farming, so the economy could not support the large settled populations that cities need.

topics.rl: Ladakh's Changpa herders move with yaks and pashmina goats across high pastures in seasonal cycles. Their tents and seasonal moves echo the Mongol gers on the steppe.

rv.summary: Mongols were pastoralists in felt gers raising horses and sheep, or poorer fur-trading hunter-gatherers in Siberia. The harsh climate limited farming, so no cities arose; society rested on patrilineal lineages and short-lived alliances.
traps: Hunter-gatherers were poorer, not richer
The 1206 quriltai does not explain the lack of cities

topics.t: The steppe and China: trade, raids and earlier confederacies
topics.h: Horses and furs for grain and iron pots: the steppe and China needed each other. When trade broke down, raids began.
p: The steppe's limited resources pushed Mongols and other nomads to trade with their sedentary neighbour, China. Nomads exchanged horses, furs and game for agricultural produce and iron utensils.

Trade benefited both sides but could be tense. When trade broke down, nomads raided farming settlements. In response, China built fortifications: the Great Wall of China, begun from the third century BCE, partly to protect farmers from nomad raids.

Earlier steppe peoples formed large confederacies too: the Hsiung-nu, Juan-juan, Huns, Uighurs and Khitan. Attila the Hun (died 453) led a powerful confederacy in Europe, but his polity did not survive his death.
Genghis Khan's achievement was different: his empire outlived him and became a lasting transcontinental power.
Why trade mattered: the steppe could not provide grain, metal tools and luxuries, so trade (or raiding) was essential for nomad survival and for the Mongol elite's wealth.

ex.q: Why was trade with China so important to the Mongols?
st: The steppe could not produce enough grain.
Metal tools and utensils came from settled societies.
Nomads had surplus horses, furs and game to exchange.
So trade filled gaps in the steppe economy; when it failed, raids followed.
ex.a: Because the steppe lacked grain and iron goods, trade with China was essential; its breakdown led to raids.

topics.rl: India's border haats with Bangladesh let people across the border exchange local produce peacefully. Exchange across ecological and political boundaries reduces conflict, a lesson the steppe-China frontier teaches too.

rv.summary: Lacking grain and iron, nomads traded horses, furs and game with China; when trade failed they raided, so China built the Great Wall from the third century BCE. Earlier confederacies like Attila's collapsed, but Genghis Khan's empire lasted.
remember: Great Wall begun from the 3rd century BCE
Attila the Hun died 453; polity didn't survive him
traps: Nomads did trade with China
The Visigoths were not a steppe confederacy

topics.t: Temujin becomes Genghis Khan
topics.h: A boy whose father was murdered, who was once captured and enslaved, grew up to be called the 'Universal Ruler'. This is Temujin's story.
p: Genghis Khan was born around 1162 near the Onon river in northern Mongolia and named Temujin. His father Yesugei was the chieftain of the Kiyat, a family of the Borjigid clan.

His father was assassinated when he was young, and his mother Oelun-eke raised Temujin, his brothers and step-brothers in hardship. Temujin was captured and enslaved in the 1170s, and his wife Borte was kidnapped soon after marriage.
He built alliances: Boghurchu became his first friend and ally; Jamuqa became his blood-brother (anda); and Ong Khan, ruler of the Kereyits, was an old ally of his father.

Jamuqa later became a rival and was defeated. Temujin then moved against the Tatars (his father's assassins), the Kereyits and Ong Khan (1203). The defeat of the Naiman people and Jamuqa in 1206 left him dominant.
At a quriltai (assembly of Mongol chiefs) in 1206, he was proclaimed Genghis Khan, the 'Oceanic Khan' or 'Universal Ruler'.

ex.q: Trace how alliances and conflicts helped Temujin rise to power.
st: Early alliances: Boghurchu, Jamuqa (anda) and Ong Khan gave him support.
He used these to defeat rivals, including Jamuqa when he turned against him.
He took on the Tatars, the Kereyits and Ong Khan.
Defeating the Naiman and Jamuqa made him dominant; the quriltai of 1206 confirmed him as Genghis Khan.
ex.a: He used alliances to build strength, then defeated rivals one by one until the 1206 quriltai proclaimed him Genghis Khan.

topics.rl: Start-up founders often begin with a few loyal partners, then grow by alliances and competition. Temujin's rise shows how networks of trust can build power from nothing.

rv.summary: Temujin, born c. 1162 near the Onon to Kiyat chief Yesugei, grew up in hardship, built alliances with Boghurchu, Jamuqa and Ong Khan, defeated rivals, and was proclaimed Genghis Khan ('Oceanic Khan') at the 1206 quriltai.
remember: Born c. 1162 near the Onon; proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206
traps: Don't confuse birth (c. 1162) with proclamation (1206)
His father's rank did not make him Genghis Khan

topics.t: Campaigns in China and Central Asia
topics.h: One rash decision by a sultan, executing Mongol envoys at Otrar, brought Genghis Khan's armies crashing into the cities of Central Asia.
p: After 1206, Genghis Khan first turned to China, then divided into three kingdoms: the Hsi Hsia of the northwest, the Chin (Jurchen) dynasty in the north, and the Sung in the south.
The Hsi Hsia were defeated, and the Chin were attacked; Peking (Beijing) was sacked in 1215 after a long siege.

In 1218 the Sultan of Khwarazm, Muhammad, executed Mongol envoys (the Otrar incident). In the campaign of 1219-1221, great cities such as Otrar, Bukhara, Samarqand, Balkh, Gurganj, Merv, Nishapur and Herat surrendered or were sacked.

At Nishapur, after a Mongol prince (Genghis Khan's son-in-law) was killed, the Mongols ordered savage reprisals. Mongol forces pursued the Sultan and his son Jalaluddin; Genghis Khan abandoned a campaign along the Indus and returned to Mongolia.
Genghis Khan died in 1227, having created a vast empire across China, Central Asia and parts of Iran.

ex.q: Explain the chain of events that led the Mongols to attack Khwarazm.
st: The Sultan of Khwarazm, Muhammad, ruled a rich state in Central Asia.
In 1218, Mongol envoys were executed at Otrar.
Genghis Khan treated this as a grave insult and provocation.
He launched the 1219-1221 campaign that sacked many cities.
ex.a: The execution of Mongol envoys at Otrar in 1218 provoked Genghis Khan's campaign against Khwarazm.

topics.rl: Even today, envoys and diplomats enjoy special protection under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which India follows. Harming envoys has always been a serious provocation.

rv.summary: Genghis Khan attacked divided China, sacking Peking in 1215. After Mongol envoys were executed at Otrar (1218), the 1219–1221 campaign devastated Khwarazm's cities. He died in 1227.
focus: Cause and course of the Khwarazm campaign
traps: Peking was not part of the Khwarazm campaign
He died in 1227, not 1206

topics.t: How the Mongols fought and how chroniclers counted
topics.h: Mongol armies used frozen rivers as highways in winter. Few enemies expected an attack in the coldest months.
p: Mongol success rested on horsemanship and archery: mounted archers moved fast and shot accurately from horseback, using light equipment.
Speed and mobility let armies cover vast distances; they also campaigned in winter, using frozen rivers as highways into enemy territory.
From campaigns in China, the Mongols learnt to use siege engines and naphtha bombardment against walled cities.

Chroniclers gave enormous figures for those killed, for example more than a million at single cities like Nishapur and Herat. These numbers were exaggerated estimates: no one could count precisely, and writers sought to convey horror.
Historians accept that destruction was real and severe, including damage to irrigation systems, but read the statistics as rhetoric rather than exact data.

ex.q: A chronicle says over 1.7 million people died at Nishapur. Give two reasons to doubt the exact figure.
st: Medieval cities rarely had populations that large.
There was no reliable counting during or after a massacre.
Writers often inflated numbers to stress horror and moral lessons.
So the figure signals great destruction, not a precise count.
ex.a: Population sizes and counting methods make it unlikely; such figures were rhetorical exaggerations of real destruction.

topics.rl: Indian Army mountain units train for winter operations in Siachen and Ladakh. Mobility, light equipment and mastery of harsh terrain still decide campaigns, as they did for the Mongols.

rv.summary: Mongol success came from mounted archery, speed, winter campaigns over frozen rivers, and siege engines and naphtha learnt in China. Chroniclers' huge casualty figures were rhetorical, though destruction was real.
remember: Siege engines and naphtha learnt from campaigns in China
traps: Winter mobility does not explain capturing walled cities
Destruction was real even if numbers were inflated

topics.t: The Mongols after Genghis Khan
topics.h: Genghis Khan died in 1227, but the empire kept growing: Russia, Baghdad and finally all of China fell to his heirs.
p: Mongol expansion after Genghis Khan came in two phases: 1236-1242, into the Russian steppes, Bulghar, Kiev, Poland and Hungary; and 1255-1300, the conquest of all of China, Iran, Iraq and Syria.
Great Khans after Genghis Khan included Ogodei, Guyuk and Mongke. Batu, grandson of Genghis Khan through Jochi, led the campaigns in Russia.
Hulegu, a grandson through Toluy, founded the Il-Khanid state in Iran and captured Baghdad in 1258.
Western expansion was halted by the defeat of Mongol forces by the Mamluks of Egypt in 1260 and by internal Mongol politics (rivalries among Genghis Khan's descendants).
Qubilai Khan completed the conquest of China (the Sung) by 1279 and ruled as founder of the Yuan dynasty. Silk Route cities such as Samarqand, Bukhara and Kashgar linked the Mongol world.

ex.q: Why did Mongol expansion in the west stop after 1260?
st: The Mamluks of Egypt defeated Mongol forces in 1260.
Rivalries among Genghis Khan's descendants divided Mongol energies.
Attention shifted to China, conquered by 1279.
So both military defeat and internal politics halted the west.
ex.a: The Mamluk victory of 1260 and internal Mongol politics checked further western expansion.

topics.rl: India's Delhi Sultanate faced repeated Mongol raids in the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries; Alauddin Khalji reorganised his army partly to resist them. The Mongol world touched Indian history directly.

rv.summary: After Genghis Khan, Mongols expanded into Russia and Eastern Europe (1236–1242), then took China, Iran, Iraq and Syria (1255–1300). Hulegu took Baghdad in 1258; the Mamluks stopped them in 1260; Qubilai founded the Yuan by 1279.
traps: The Mamluks defeated the Mongols, not the reverse
Batu led Russian campaigns; Hulegu took Baghdad

topics.t: A new army and the four ulus
topics.h: Genghis Khan deliberately broke up old tribes and mixed their men into new units. Loyalty to him replaced loyalty to clan.
p: Mongol and other nomad men were organised into a decimal army: units of 10, 100, 1,000 and roughly 10,000 soldiers (tumen). This followed an old steppe tradition.
Genghis Khan broke up old tribal groupings and distributed their members into new military units. A soldier who tried to move away without permission was severely punished.

Those who had served him loyally for years were given the title noyan, commanders of the new army. Old relationships such as anda (blood-brother) and naukar (bondsman or companion) bound followers to him.

Conquered territories were divided among his four sons into ulus (shares of dominion): Jochi, Chaghatai, Ogodei and Toluy. Ogodei was named Great Khan; Toluy, the youngest, received the Mongol homeland.
Why restructure? Old tribal loyalties caused feuds and weak, short-lived confederacies. New mixed units created loyalty to Genghis Khan and his family, turning many tribes into one disciplined army.

ex.q: A Mongol army had 3 tumens. Using the decimal system, roughly how many soldiers is that?
