qa.e: A is true; R is false, because Greek, Aramaic, Coptic, Punic, Berber and Celtic were also spoken.

qa.q: What were amphorae used for in the Roman world?
qa.a: Carrying liquids such as wine and olive oil
qa.e: Amphorae were containers for wine, olive oil and similar goods.

qa.q: Monte Testaccio in Rome is made of the remains of about how many vessels?
qa.e: It contains the remains of over 50 million amphorae.

qa.q: Dressel 20 containers carried:
qa.e: Dressel 20 amphorae carried olive oil from Spain.

qa.q: The name 'Dressel 20' comes from:
qa.e: The type is named after the archaeologist who classified these forms.

qa.q: Which region was in modern Tunisia and famous for its fertility?
qa.e: Byzacium in Tunisia was a fertile region; Campania is in Italy, Galilee in Palestine.

qa.q: Transhumance in the Numidian countryside refers to:
qa.a: Pastoral communities moving seasonally with flocks
qa.e: Pastoral and semi-nomadic groups moved with their herds; Roman estates reduced their space.

qa.q: Which technology was used on a massive scale in Spanish gold and silver mines?
qa.e: Hydraulic mining reached levels not matched until the nineteenth century.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Roman economy was highly developed. Reason (R): Augustus founded the Principate in 27 BCE.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the founding of the Principate does not explain the economy's sophistication; its infrastructure and money use do.

qa.q: In Augustus's time, about how many slaves were there in Italy?
qa.e: About 3 million slaves lived among Italy's 7.5 million people.

qa.q: Why did the supply of slaves decline in the first century?
qa.a: Peace reduced the number of war captives
qa.e: With fewer wars, fewer captives were available as slaves.

qa.q: How did slave owners respond to the fall in slave supply?
qa.a: Through slave breeding or using cheaper free labour
qa.e: They turned to breeding slaves or hiring wage labour.

qa.q: Why was free labour used extensively in public works at Rome?
qa.a: Slaves had to be fed and housed all year
qa.e: Maintaining slaves year-round was costly; hired labour could be dismissed.

qa.q: Columella was:
qa.a: A first-century agricultural writer from southern Spain
qa.e: Columella wrote on agriculture and labour management.

qa.q: Why did Columella advise keeping twice as many tools as needed?
qa.a: So production was continuous and slave labour-time not lost
qa.e: Lost labour time cost more than spare tools.

qa.q: A law of 398 shows that some workers were:
qa.a: Branded so they could be recognised if they ran away
qa.e: Branding reveals the harsh control of workers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Slavery had disappeared from Italy by Augustus's time. Reason (R): Free labour was used extensively in public works at Rome.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because Italy had about 3 million slaves under Augustus; R is true.

qa.q: Which Roman historian described the social groups of the early empire, including the 'plebs sordida'?
qa.e: Tacitus gave this description of early imperial society.

qa.q: What happened to senators and equites in the late empire?
qa.a: They merged into a unified, expanded aristocracy
qa.e: The two groups merged into one aristocracy.

qa.q: Which group was often more powerful than the late Roman aristocracy despite humbler origins?
qa.e: Military elites, drawn mostly from non-aristocratic backgrounds, held great power.

qa.q: Who made up the 'middle' class of the late empire?
qa.a: People in the bureaucracy and army, and prosperous merchants and farmers
qa.e: Imperial servants and prosperous merchants and farmers formed this group.

qa.q: Constantine's solidus was a coin of:
qa.e: The solidus contained 4.5 grams of pure gold and was minted in huge numbers.

qa.q: According to Olympiodorus, many great houses of Rome earned per year up to:
qa.e: He recorded incomes of up to 4,000 lbs of gold, not counting produce consumed directly.

qa.q: Which of these belonged to the lower classes (humiliores)?
qa.a: Migrant workers in harvests and construction
qa.e: Rural labourers, migrant workers, artisans and slaves made up the lower classes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The late Roman administration was affected by corruption. Reason (R): Historians praised late Roman tax collectors for their honesty.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because sources complain of the greed of tax collectors.

qa.q: The term 'Late Antiquity' refers to roughly which period?
qa.e: Late Antiquity covers the fourth to seventh centuries.

qa.q: Which emperor separated civil from military functions?
qa.e: Diocletian reorganised administration this way and gave military commanders more autonomy.

qa.q: Military commanders given greater autonomy under Diocletian were called:
qa.e: The duces (singular dux) were military commanders.

qa.q: Constantinople was built on the site of:
qa.e: Constantinople stood on the site of Byzantium, modern Istanbul.

qa.q: Constantinople was surrounded on how many sides by the sea?
qa.e: The sea surrounded the city on three sides, aiding defence.

qa.q: Which emperor introduced the gold solidus?
qa.e: Constantine introduced the solidus.

qa.q: Which developments show economic growth in the late empire?
qa.a: Investment in oil presses, glass factories and water-mills
qa.e: Archaeology reveals rural investment and revived trade with the East.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The late Roman economy showed growth in many areas. Reason (R): Constantinople was built on the site of Byzantium.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the site of the new capital does not explain economic growth, which came from monetary stability and population growth.

qa.q: Roman traditional religion before Christianisation was best described as:
qa.a: Polytheistic, with many cults like Jupiter, Juno, Minerva and Mars
qa.e: Romans worshipped many gods; Judaism also existed in the empire.

qa.q: Who became the most important figures in the Christian community in the late empire?
qa.e: Bishops were often very powerful in the Christian community.

qa.q: Which Germanic group set up a kingdom in Spain?
qa.e: The Visigoths ruled Spain; the Franks ruled Gaul.

qa.q: Which Germanic group set up a kingdom in Gaul?
qa.e: The Franks founded a kingdom in Gaul (later France).

qa.q: Justinian reigned in the East from:
qa.e: Justinian ruled 527-565, a high point of eastern prosperity.

qa.q: Which part of the Roman Empire collapsed politically under Germanic invasions?
qa.e: The western empire fragmented; the eastern empire survived and prospered.

qa.q: In the seventh century, Arab armies conquered large parts of the eastern Roman provinces and:
qa.e: The Sasanian empire of Iran also fell to the Arab conquests.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Roman world became Christian overnight under Constantine. Reason (R): Bishops became powerful figures in the Christian community.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because Christianisation was gradual over the fourth and fifth centuries; R is true.

qa.q: Why does the phrase 'nomadic empire' seem contradictory?
qa.a: Nomads are mobile, while empires usually need settled control of territory
qa.e: Empires are associated with settled administration; nomads with movement.

qa.q: In which centuries did the Mongols build their transcontinental empire?
qa.e: The Mongol empire arose in the thirteenth century and lasted into the fourteenth.

qa.q: Who wrote most of the sources about the Mongols?
qa.a: City-based chroniclers, travellers and court historians
qa.e: Most accounts come from urban literate writers outside the nomadic world.

qa.q: The word 'barbarian' comes from the Greek 'barbaros', which meant:
qa.e: To Greeks, a barbaros was a non-Greek whose speech sounded like babble.

qa.q: Which groups did the Romans call barbarians?
qa.e: Romans applied the term to peoples like Germanic tribes, Gauls and Huns.

qa.q: A medieval chronicle claims impossibly large numbers were killed in a Mongol siege. The best historical response is to:
qa.a: Treat the figure as possibly inflated and check other evidence
qa.e: Historians weigh bias and compare sources rather than accept or reject blindly.

qa.q: Why were many city-based writers hostile to the Mongols?
qa.a: They saw nomads as destroyers of settled urban life
qa.e: Writers from settled societies viewed nomads as threats to cities and order.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Historians must read medieval accounts of the Mongols critically. Reason (R): Most accounts of the Mongols were written by Mongol herders themselves.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because most accounts were by city-based writers, often hostile to nomads.

qa.q: From which deity did Genghis Khan believe he had a mandate to rule the world?
qa.e: He believed the Eternal Sky (Tengri) had given him a mandate.

qa.q: Who described the capture of Bukhara in 1220?
qa.e: The Persian chronicler Juwaini wrote this account.

qa.q: In which year was Bukhara captured by the Mongols?
qa.e: Bukhara fell in 1220 during the campaign against Khwarazm.

qa.q: What did Genghis Khan tell the rich residents of Bukhara, according to Juwaini?
qa.a: That he was God's punishment for their great sins
qa.e: He said their sins had brought God's punishment, in the form of himself.

qa.q: Between 1236 and 1241, Mongol armies reached as far as the outskirts of:
qa.e: They moved through Russia, Poland and Hungary towards Vienna.

qa.q: The survivor's phrase 'They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed' stresses the Mongols':
qa.e: It sums up a swift, violent conquest.

qa.q: Imagine you were a resident of Bukhara hearing Genghis Khan's speech. Which reaction is most historically plausible?
qa.a: Fear and shock at being blamed and threatened
qa.e: The speech came after conquest and blamed the residents, likely causing fear.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Genghis Khan saw his conquests as justified. Reason (R): He believed he had a mandate from the Eternal Sky to rule the world.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; his belief in a divine mandate explains how he justified conquest.

qa.q: Where did the Mongol hunter-gatherers live?
qa.a: In the Siberian forests to the north
qa.e: Hunter-gatherers lived in the Siberian forests north of the pastoralists.

qa.q: Which animals did Mongol pastoralists mainly raise?
qa.a: Horses and sheep, and to a lesser extent goats and camels
qa.e: Horses and sheep were most important.

qa.q: What were Mongol felt tents called?
qa.e: Gers were portable felt tents suited to seasonal movement.

qa.q: Compared with the pastoralists, the hunter-gatherers were generally:
qa.a: Poorer, living by trade in furs
qa.e: Hunter-gatherers were poorer and traded furs.

qa.q: Why did the Mongols not depend on agriculture?
qa.a: The harsh climate allowed farming only in limited seasons
qa.e: Long winters and short dry summers limited farming.

qa.q: Mongol society was organised on the basis of:
qa.e: Descent was traced through the male line.

qa.q: Steppe alliances and confederacies were usually:
qa.e: They formed for defence or raids but rarely lasted long.

qa.q: Assertion (A): No cities emerged on the Mongolian steppe. Reason (R): Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan at the quriltai of 1206.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the 1206 quriltai does not explain the absence of cities; the limited steppe economy does.

qa.q: What did nomads typically trade to China?
qa.e: Steppe products like horses, furs and game were exchanged for Chinese grain and iron.

qa.q: What did nomads get from China?
qa.e: They obtained grain and iron goods that the steppe could not produce.

qa.q: The Great Wall of China was built partly to:
qa.e: It was a defence against raiders from the steppe.

qa.q: When did construction of the Great Wall begin?
qa.e: Fortifications began from the third century BCE.

qa.q: Which leader of an earlier steppe confederacy died in 453?
qa.e: Attila the Hun died in 453; his polity did not outlive him.

qa.q: Which of these was NOT an earlier steppe confederacy?
qa.e: The Visigoths were a Germanic group in Europe; the others were steppe peoples.

qa.q: How did Genghis Khan's achievement differ from Attila's?
qa.e: Attila's polity collapsed after him; the Mongol empire expanded further.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nomads never traded with China. Reason (R): The Great Wall of China was built partly to keep out nomad raiders.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because nomads traded horses and furs for grain and iron; R is true.

qa.q: Genghis Khan was born around:
qa.e: Temujin was born around 1162; 1206 is when he became Genghis Khan.

qa.q: What was Genghis Khan's original name?
qa.e: He was named Temujin at birth.

qa.q: Temujin's father, Yesugei, was the chieftain of the:
qa.e: Yesugei headed the Kiyat, a family of the Borjigid clan.

qa.q: Who raised Temujin after his father was assassinated?
qa.e: His mother brought up Temujin and his brothers in hardship.

qa.q: Jamuqa was Temujin's:
qa.a: Blood-brother (anda), who later became a rival
qa.e: Jamuqa was his anda who later turned against him and was defeated.

qa.q: What does 'Genghis Khan' mean?
qa.e: The title means Oceanic Khan or Universal Ruler.

qa.q: In which year was Temujin proclaimed Genghis Khan at a quriltai?
qa.e: The quriltai of 1206 proclaimed him Genghis Khan.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The quriltai of 1206 proclaimed Temujin as Genghis Khan. Reason (R): Temujin's father Yesugei was a chieftain of the Kiyat.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but his father's position does not explain the 1206 proclamation, which followed Temujin's victories over rivals.

qa.q: Peking (Beijing) was sacked by the Mongols in:
qa.e: Peking fell in 1215 after a long siege.

qa.q: Which dynasty ruled northern China when Genghis Khan attacked?
qa.e: The Chin, a Jurchen dynasty, ruled north China; the Sung ruled the south.

qa.q: The Hsi Hsia were a people of:
qa.e: The Hsi Hsia ruled north-western China and were defeated early.

qa.q: What provoked the Mongol campaign against Khwarazm?
qa.a: The execution of Mongol envoys at Otrar in 1218
qa.e: The killing of Mongol envoys was a serious provocation.

qa.q: Which city was NOT sacked in the campaign against Khwarazm?
qa.e: Peking was in China, taken in 1215; the others were Central Asian cities.

qa.q: When did Genghis Khan die?
qa.e: He died in 1227.

qa.q: Who was the Sultan of Khwarazm whose state the Mongols attacked?
qa.e: Sultan Muhammad ruled Khwarazm; his son Jalaluddin was also pursued.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Mongol campaign of 1219-1221 devastated many Central Asian cities. Reason (R): Cities such as Bukhara, Samarqand, Merv and Nishapur were sacked or surrendered.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the list of cities shows the scale of the campaign.

qa.q: Which skill was central to Mongol military success?
qa.e: Riding and shooting from horseback gave speed and firepower.

qa.q: How did the Mongols use winter to their advantage?
qa.a: They used frozen rivers as highways
qa.e: Frozen rivers became routes into enemy territory.

qa.q: From which campaigns did the Mongols learn to use siege engines and naphtha bombardment?
qa.e: Experience in China taught them siege warfare.

qa.q: Why were Mongol armies so mobile?
qa.a: Horses, light equipment and skilled riders
qa.e: Cavalry and light gear allowed rapid movement.

qa.q: Why do historians doubt the exact casualty figures of medieval chroniclers?
qa.a: They were inflated estimates meant to stress horror
qa.e: Writers had no way to count and wished to emphasise destruction.

qa.q: What is the balanced historical view of Mongol destruction?
qa.a: It was real and severe, but the statistics were exaggerated
qa.e: Destruction occurred, but numbers in chronicles are rhetorical.

qa.q: Naphtha bombardment refers to:
qa.a: Using burning material to attack cities
qa.e: Naphtha, an inflammable substance, was hurled at enemy defences.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Mongols could capture walled cities. Reason (R): Mongol armies used frozen rivers as highways in winter campaigns.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but winter mobility does not explain success against walls; siege engines and naphtha bombardment do.

qa.q: The first phase of Mongol expansion after Genghis Khan (1236-1242) was directed towards:
qa.e: This phase moved into the Russian steppes and Eastern Europe.

qa.q: The second phase (1255-1300) brought the conquest of:
qa.e: The second phase completed the conquest of China and took Iran, Iraq and Syria.

qa.q: Who captured Baghdad in 1258?
qa.e: Hulegu, founder of the Il-Khanid state, took Baghdad.

qa.q: Who defeated the Mongols in 1260, checking their western expansion?
qa.e: The Mamluks of Egypt defeated the Mongols in 1260.

qa.q: By which year had Qubilai Khan completed the conquest of China?
qa.e: The Sung were finally defeated by 1279.

qa.q: Qubilai Khan ruled China as founder of which dynasty?
qa.e: Qubilai founded the Yuan dynasty.

qa.q: The Il-Khanid state was founded in:
qa.e: Hulegu founded the Il-Khanid state in Iran.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mongol expansion westwards stopped after 1260. Reason (R): The Mongols defeated the Mamluks of Egypt in 1260.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because the Mamluks defeated the Mongols in 1260.

qa.q: A Mongol tumen consisted of about:
qa.e: The tumen was the largest unit, about 10,000 men.

qa.q: How many soldiers were there in 5 units of 100?
Why did Genghis Khan break up old tribal groups in his army?
qa.a: To replace clan loyalty with loyalty to himself
qa.e: Mixing tribes into new units weakened old loyalties and feuds.

qa.q: The title noyan was given to:
qa.e: Old loyal followers were rewarded as noyan.

qa.q: The four sons among whom Genghis Khan divided the ulus were:
qa.e: His four sons were Jochi, Chaghatai, Ogodei and Toluy.

qa.q: Which son was designated Great Khan after Genghis Khan?
qa.e: Ogodei became the Great Khan.

qa.q: What did a soldier risk if he moved away from his unit without permission?
qa.e: Leaving one's unit was harshly punished to keep discipline.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Genghis Khan's army was highly disciplined. Reason (R): Old tribal groups were broken up and soldiers could not leave their units without permission.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; restructuring and strict rules explain the discipline.

qa.q: The Mongol courier system was called the:
qa.e: The yam was the relay system for fast communication.

qa.q: How was the yam financed?
qa.a: By a levy called qubcur paid by Mongol nomads
qa.e: Nomads contributed a levy from their herds.

qa.q: A paiza or gerege was:
qa.e: It worked like a passport for safe travel.

qa.q: The tax that merchants paid for safe passage was called:
qa.e: Merchants paid baj; qubcur was the nomads' levy for the yam.

qa.q: 'Pax Mongolica' refers to:
qa.a: The safety of trade routes and exchange under Mongol rule
qa.e: It describes the security of trade across the Mongol empire.

qa.q: William of Rubruck visited the court of which Great Khan?
qa.e: He was at Mongke's court in 1254.

qa.q: William of Rubruck was sent by:
qa.e: The French king Louis IX sent him.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade along the Silk Route reached its peak under the Mongols. Reason (R): The Mongols provided safe-conduct passes and protected routes across a unified empire.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; protection and passes explain the trade boom.

qa.q: Why did the Mongols recruit Chinese, Persian and Uighur administrators?
qa.a: They needed skilled officials to govern settled lands
qa.e: Governing large settled populations required experienced civil administrators.

qa.q: Yeh-lu Ch'u-ts'ai persuaded Ogodei that:
qa.a: Taxing peasants was more profitable than turning farmland into pasture
qa.e: He argued for taxing productive farmers rather than ruining them.

qa.q: Rashiduddin served as wazir to:
qa.e: Rashiduddin was Ghazan's wazir and drafted his famous speech.

qa.q: Ghazan Khan was the Il-Khan from:
qa.e: Ghazan ruled the Il-Khanid state from 1295 to 1304.

qa.q: Ghazan Khan's speech to his commanders was drafted by his wazir:
qa.e: Rashiduddin, Ghazan's wazir and historian, drafted the speech.

qa.q: What was the main message of Ghazan Khan's speech to his commanders?
qa.e: He warned that harassing peasants would ruin the state's prosperity.

qa.q: Why did pastoralists and peasants have conflicting interests?
qa.a: Herders wanted pasture and booty, while peasants needed stable fields
qa.e: Using land for grazing or raids clashed with settled farming.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Mongol state had to protect peasants in conquered lands. Reason (R): Ghazan Khan urged his commanders to plunder the peasantry.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because Ghazan urged commanders not to harass peasants.

qa.q: The term 'yasaq' originally meant:
qa.e: Yasaq meant law, decree or order; later yasa meant the legal code.

qa.q: By the mid-thirteenth century, 'yasa' had come to mean:
qa.a: The legal code believed to be formulated by Genghis Khan
qa.e: It became the name of Genghis Khan's legal code.

qa.q: The details we know about the early yasa mostly concern:
qa.a: Administration: the hunt, the army and the postal system
qa.e: The known details relate to administrative regulations.

qa.q: How did the yasa help the Mongols?
qa.a: It gave them a shared identity and legitimacy over subjects
qa.e: It expressed loyalty to Genghis Khan's traditions and authority.

qa.q: Which sixteenth-century ruler of Bukhara was described as acting 'according to the yasa'?
qa.e: 'Abdullah Khan, an Uzbek ruler, was linked to the yasa by a chronicler.

qa.q: What does the 'Abdullah Khan example show about the yasa?
qa.a: Later rulers reinterpreted it as a symbol of Genghisid tradition
qa.e: Its meaning stretched to legitimise practices in a very different context.

qa.q: Over roughly how many centuries can historians trace changing meanings of the yasa, from 1206 to 'Abdullah Khan's time?
qa.e: From the thirteenth to the sixteenth century is about four centuries.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The meaning of yasa never changed after 1206. Reason (R): A sixteenth-century writer described 'Abdullah Khan of Bukhara as acting according to the yasa of Genghis Khan.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because yasa shifted from decree to legal code to symbol of legitimacy; R is true.

qa.q: How do conquered peoples' chronicles mainly portray Genghis Khan?
qa.a: As a conqueror and destroyer of cities
qa.e: City-based chronicles stress destruction.

qa.q: How is Genghis Khan viewed in modern Mongolia?
qa.e: Mongolians honour him as the founder of their nation.

qa.q: Mongol rule is described as multi-ethnic, multi-lingual and:
qa.e: The empire included many peoples, languages and faiths.

qa.q: Timur, who was not a direct descendant of Genghis Khan, called himself:
qa.e: He married a Genghisid princess and took the title guregen.

qa.q: The Mughal emperor Babur descended from Genghis Khan through his:
qa.e: Babur was a Genghisid on his mother's side and a Timurid on his father's side.

qa.q: When did Mongolia revive Genghis Khan as a national symbol, after decades of Soviet influence?
qa.e: Post-Soviet Mongolia in the 1990s celebrated him as a national hero.

qa.q: Which statement best describes how historians should view Genghis Khan?
qa.a: His conquests were destructive, but he also built a lasting, diverse empire, and his memory differs by community
qa.e: A balanced view weighs destruction, achievement and how memory varies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Later rulers like Timur and Babur emphasised links with Genghis Khan. Reason (R): Mongol rule was multi-ethnic, multi-lingual and multi-religious.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the empire's diversity does not explain why later rulers claimed links; the prestige and legitimacy of Genghisid descent does.

qa.q: Which was the first order in medieval European society?
qa.e: The clergy were the first order, the nobility the second and peasants the third.

qa.q: The three orders described society in western Europe roughly between the:
qa.e: The three orders framework applies to the ninth to sixteenth centuries.

qa.q: Marc Bloch was a scholar from:
qa.e: Marc Bloch was French.

qa.q: Marc Bloch's famous book on medieval society is called:
qa.e: Feudal Society studied European society from about 900 to 1300.

qa.q: What was distinctive about Marc Bloch's approach?
qa.a: He stressed geography and social relations, not just politics
qa.e: Bloch broadened history to include society and environment.

qa.q: Which source would best help a historian study medieval births, marriages and deaths?
qa.e: Churches recorded these life events.

qa.q: Marc Bloch died in:
qa.e: He was killed by the Nazis in 1944.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Historians can reconstruct the lives of ordinary medieval people. Reason (R): Records of landownership, prices, legal cases and church registers survive.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; such records make social history possible.

qa.q: The word 'feudalism' comes from 'feud', a German word meaning:
qa.e: Feud means a piece of land.

qa.q: Feudalism describes which kinds of relationships in medieval Europe?
qa.e: It covers many dimensions of medieval life.

qa.q: In return for military service and loyalty, a vassal received from his lord:
qa.e: Land was granted for loyalty and service.

qa.q: The part of the manor kept for the lord's own use was called the:
qa.e: The demesne was the lord's own land, cultivated by peasants' labour.

qa.q: What did the lord provide to peasants in exchange for their labour?
qa.e: The lord offered protection; he also exercised judicial control.

qa.q: In the feudal chain, peasants were vassals of:
qa.e: Big landowners were vassals of the king; peasants were vassals of landowners.

qa.q: Which statement about lords' judicial power is correct?
qa.a: Lords had extensive judicial control over peasants
qa.e: Lords held courts and controlled justice on their estates.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Peasants under feudalism had to work on the lord's land. Reason (R): Lords gave peasants nothing in return for their labour.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because lords provided military protection in exchange.

qa.q: Which Germanic tribe gave its name to France?
qa.e: The Franks gave their name to Gaul, which became France.

qa.q: France was earlier a Roman province called:
qa.e: Gaul became France.

qa.q: In which year was Charlemagne given the title of Holy Roman Emperor?
qa.e: The Pope crowned Charlemagne in 800.

qa.q: Who gave Charlemagne the title of Holy Roman Emperor?
qa.e: The Pope crowned him to secure his support.

qa.q: William, who conquered England in 1066, was the Duke of:
qa.e: William was Duke of Normandy in northern France.

qa.q: After the Norman conquest, the Anglo-Saxons in England mostly became:
qa.e: Normans became lords; Anglo-Saxons became tenants.

qa.q: Which is a feature of early feudal society in France?
qa.a: Close ties between kings and the Church
qa.e: French kings were closely allied with the Church.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Frankish kings had strong ties with the Church. Reason (R): In 800 the Pope gave Charlemagne the title of Holy Roman Emperor to secure his support.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the coronation shows and explains the close bond.

qa.q: Nobles in medieval Europe were vassals of:
qa.e: Nobles accepted the king as their lord (seigneur).

qa.q: The word 'seigneur' means:
qa.e: A seigneur was a senior or lord to whom the vassal owed loyalty.

qa.q: What did a vassal sometimes receive as a symbol of the land granted to him?
qa.e: A written charter, a staff or a clod of earth could symbolise the grant.

qa.q: Where were the vows between lord and vassal often taken?
qa.e: Vows were exchanged in elaborate church ceremonies.

qa.q: Which was NOT a privilege of the nobility?
qa.e: The tithe was collected by the Church; the other three were noble privileges.

qa.q: A noble had control over his property:
qa.e: Nobles had absolute control over property, in perpetuity.

qa.q: Could a noble have vassals of his own?
qa.a: Yes; he was lord of the people settled on his land
qa.e: Lordship ran down the chain: nobles had their own vassals.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The nobility played a central role in medieval society. Reason (R): Gaul came to be called France after the Franks.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the origin of France's name does not explain the nobility's role, which came from land and privileges.

qa.q: A small manorial estate could have about:
qa.e: Small manors had about a dozen families; larger ones fifty or sixty.

qa.q: Which item usually had to be obtained from outside the manor?
qa.e: Salt, millstones and metalware came from outside.

qa.q: Who maintained the lord's implements and repaired weapons on the estate?
qa.e: Estate craftsmen handled tools and weapons.

qa.q: Which feature of the manor was mainly for defence?
qa.e: Castles or fortified houses defended the estate.

qa.q: Why was the manor not fully self-sufficient?
qa.a: It needed salt, millstones, metalware and luxuries from outside
qa.e: Some essentials and luxuries had to be brought in.

qa.q: What did children on the manor often do?
qa.e: Children worked in wine-presses; women spun and wove.

qa.q: From the thirteenth century, some castles were enlarged to become:
qa.e: Castles grew into homes for knightly families.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Lords who wanted luxurious lifestyles had to obtain goods from other places. Reason (R): Rich furnishings, musical instruments and ornaments were not produced locally on the manor.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; local production could not supply luxuries.

qa.q: From which century did knights grow in importance in Europe?
qa.e: From the ninth century, frequent wars needed good cavalry.

qa.q: The land given by a lord to a knight was called a:
qa.e: A fief was land granted in return for service.

qa.q: A knight's fief could extend to about:
qa.e: Fiefs were 1,000-2,000 acres or more.

qa.q: Which feature was typically part of a knight's fief?
qa.e: Fiefs had a house, church, water-mill and wine-press.

qa.q: What did a knight give his lord in return for the fief?
qa.a: A regular fee and a promise to fight for him
qa.e: The knight paid a fee and promised military service.

qa.q: Could a knight serve more than one lord?
qa.a: Yes, but his foremost loyalty was to his own lord
qa.e: Multiple service was possible, but his own lord came first.

qa.q: From the twelfth century, who travelled from manor to manor singing of brave kings and knights?
qa.e: Minstrels sang these partly historical, partly invented tales.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Knights became less important in the later Middle Ages. Reason (R): Gunpowder was unknown in Europe until the twentieth century.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because gunpowder weapons spread in Europe from the late Middle Ages and helped end the knights' dominance.

qa.q: Who was the head of the Catholic Church in medieval Europe?
qa.e: The Pope in Rome headed the Church.

qa.q: The tithe was a share of a peasant's produce equal to:
qa.e: The Church took one-tenth of the year's produce.

qa.q: A peasant produced 80 bushels of wheat. How many bushels was his tithe?
qa.e: One-tenth of 80 is 8.

qa.q: Which group could become priests in the medieval Church?
qa.a: Unmarried free men without physical disability
qa.e: Serfs, the physically disabled and women were barred, and priests could not marry, so only unmarried free men without physical disability qualified.

qa.q: Bishops in medieval Europe were considered:
qa.e: With vast estates and palaces, bishops were the religious nobility.

qa.q: Why does the date of Easter change every year?
qa.a: It is calculated by the lunar calendar
qa.e: Easter replaced a spring festival dated by the lunar calendar.

qa.q: The act of kneeling in prayer with hands clasped was a replica of:
qa.a: A knight taking vows of loyalty to his lord
qa.e: Church ritual borrowed the forms of feudal homage.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Christmas and Easter became important festivals in medieval Europe. Reason (R): Bishops had vast estates and lived in grand palaces.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but bishops' wealth does not explain the importance of the festivals; their blending with older seasonal festivals does.

qa.q: Where did monks live?
qa.a: In abbeys or monasteries, often far from towns
qa.e: Monks lived in religious communities apart from society.

qa.q: The monastery of St Benedict was founded in Italy in:
qa.e: St Benedict's monastery dates to 529; Cluny to 910.

qa.q: Cluny, a famous monastery, was founded in 910 in:
qa.e: Cluny was in Burgundy.

qa.q: According to St Benedict's rules, monks should NOT:
qa.e: No monk was to own private property.

qa.q: Which rule of St Benedict explains why monks did manual labour?
qa.a: Idleness is the enemy of the soul
qa.e: Keeping busy with work and reading protected the soul.

qa.q: Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179) is remembered as:
qa.a: A gifted musician who developed community singing of prayers
qa.e: This abbess shaped church music.

qa.q: Friars differed from monks because they:
qa.a: Moved from place to place preaching and living on charity
qa.e: Friars worked among people rather than in enclosed monasteries.

qa.q: Assertion (A): By the fourteenth century, monasteries faced criticism. Reason (R): Writers like Langland and Chaucer contrasted simple faith with the wealth and worldliness of some monks, nuns and friars.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these writings show and explain the criticism.

qa.q: The word 'serf' is derived from the verb:
qa.e: Serf comes from 'to serve'.

qa.q: How did free peasants hold their farms?
qa.e: Free peasants were tenants who owed services to the lord.

qa.q: The work free peasants did on the lord's land on set days was called:
qa.e: Labour-rent went directly to the lord.

qa.q: The taille was:
qa.a: A direct tax kings sometimes imposed on peasants
qa.e: The taille was a royal tax; clergy and nobles were exempt.

qa.q: Who was exempt from the taille?
qa.e: The first two orders did not pay it.

qa.q: Which was true of serfs?
qa.a: They could not leave the estate without the lord's permission
qa.e: Serfs were tied to the estate and controlled by the lord.

qa.q: Serfs had to grind their flour at:
qa.e: Lords claimed monopolies over mills, ovens and wine-presses.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Serfs could leave the lord's estate whenever they wished. Reason (R): Serfs had to use the lord's mill and oven.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because serfs needed the lord's permission to leave; R is true.

qa.q: Feudalism developed in England from the:
qa.e: It developed after the Norman conquest of 1066.

qa.q: The name 'England' comes from:
qa.e: England means land of the Angles.

qa.q: The Angles and Saxons settled in England in the:
qa.e: They arrived from central Europe in the sixth century.

qa.q: About how many Norman nobles received land from William I?
qa.e: William distributed land to about 180 Norman nobles.

qa.q: What did the Norman lords have to supply to the king?
qa.e: As chief tenants, they provided knights for the king.

qa.q: What was forbidden to lords in England?
qa.e: Private warfare was banned, keeping the king's control.

qa.q: After the Norman conquest, the Anglo-Saxon peasants became:
qa.a: Tenants of various levels of landowners
qa.e: They became tenants under the new Norman landowners.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The English king retained strong control over the lords after 1066. Reason (R): The Angles and Saxons had settled in England in the sixth century.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the earlier settlement does not explain royal control; land held as chief tenants and the ban on private warfare do.

qa.q: From which century did Europe enter a warmer phase that helped agriculture?
qa.e: A warm phase from the eleventh century lengthened growing seasons.

qa.q: The early medieval wooden plough was ineffective because it:
qa.a: Could only scratch the surface of the soil
qa.e: It could not bring out the soil's natural productivity.

qa.q: What was the advantage of the heavy iron-tipped plough with a mould-board?
qa.a: It dug deeper and turned the topsoil properly
qa.e: Deeper ploughing used soil nutrients better.

qa.q: The shoulder harness replaced the neck harness so that:
qa.e: Shoulder harnesses let animals pull heavier loads.

qa.q: In the three-field system, the spring field was used for:
qa.a: Peas, beans and lentils, and oats and barley for horses
qa.e: Spring sowing included pulses for people and oats and barley for horses.

qa.q: Under the three-field system, what fraction of a farm lay fallow each year?
qa.e: One of three fields was fallow each year.

qa.q: By how many millions did Europe's population rise from 1000 (42 million) to 1300 (73 million)?
qa.e: 73 − 42 = 31 million.

qa.q: Assertion (A): From the eleventh century, many lords asked peasants for rent in cash instead of labour services. Reason (R): Economic transactions were becoming more money-based as trade grew.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the spread of money explains the shift to cash rents.

qa.q: Why did towns begin to grow in Europe from the eleventh century?
qa.a: Agricultural surplus and trade created a need for market centres
qa.e: Surplus grain and trade led to fairs and market towns.

qa.q: What did the saying 'Town air makes free' mean?
qa.a: A serf who hid in a town for a year and a day became free
qa.e: Escaping to a town could end serfdom.

qa.q: Medieval guilds were associations that:
qa.a: Controlled the quality, price and sale of products
qa.e: Guilds regulated each craft or industry.

qa.q: In towns, instead of labour services, people:
qa.a: Paid tax to the lord who owned the land
qa.e: Townspeople paid tax rather than services.

qa.q: Bigger medieval towns had populations of about:
qa.e: Large towns had about 30,000 people.

qa.q: Large cathedrals began to be built in France from the:
qa.e: Cathedral building took off from the twelfth century.

qa.q: Why were stained-glass windows important in cathedrals?
qa.a: They told Bible stories in pictures for people who could not read
qa.e: Pictures in glass let non-literate people 'read' the Bible stories.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Small towns developed around cathedrals. Reason (R): Stained-glass windows told Bible stories in pictures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but stained glass does not explain town growth; cathedrals becoming pilgrimage centres does.

qa.q: The severe famines that hit Europe occurred in:
qa.e: Famines struck in 1315-1317; the Black Death came in 1347-1350.

qa.q: The Black Death struck western Europe in:
qa.e: The plague raged in 1347-1350.

qa.q: How did the bubonic plague reach Europe's ports?
qa.e: Rats on ships carried the infection.

qa.q: About what share of Europe's population died in the Black Death, by modern estimates?
qa.e: Around 20 per cent died, with some places losing up to 40 per cent.

qa.q: Europe's population fell from 73 million (1300) to 45 million (1400). By how many millions did it fall?
qa.e: 73 − 45 = 28 million.

qa.q: Why did wages rise after the Black Death?
qa.a: There was a severe shortage of labour
qa.e: Fewer workers meant higher demand for labour.

qa.q: The Jacquerie of 1358 was a peasant revolt in:
qa.e: The Jacquerie was in France; England's Peasants' Revolt was in 1381.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade suffered in fourteenth-century Europe. Reason (R): Silver mines in Austria and Serbia produced record amounts of silver in the fourteenth century.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because silver output fell, causing a shortage of metal money.

qa.q: Which technological change weakened knights and castles?
qa.e: Guns and cannon made armoured cavalry and castles vulnerable.

qa.q: Which ruler was a 'new monarch' in France?
qa.e: Louis XI ruled France; Henry VII England; Maximilian Austria.

qa.q: Henry VII was a new monarch in:
qa.e: Henry VII ruled England.

qa.q: Which joint rulers are counted among the new monarchs of Spain?
qa.e: Isabella and Ferdinand ruled Spain.

qa.q: Which was a key feature of the new monarchies?
qa.a: Standing armies, a permanent bureaucracy and national taxation
qa.e: Kings centralised military and financial power.

qa.q: How did many nobles survive the rise of new monarchies?
qa.a: By becoming loyal courtiers and officials
qa.e: Nobles transformed themselves into royal loyalists.

qa.q: Charles I of England was executed in:
qa.e: Charles I was executed in 1649 after ruling without Parliament.

qa.q: Assertion (A): England's Parliament had only one house. Reason (R): Charles I was executed in 1649.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because Parliament had the House of Lords and the House of Commons; R is true.

qa.q: The word 'Renaissance' literally means:
qa.e: Renaissance means rebirth, the revival of classical learning.

qa.q: Who wrote The Civilisation of the Renaissance in Italy?
qa.e: The Swiss historian Jacob Burckhardt wrote it in 1860.

qa.q: Burckhardt's book was published in:
qa.e: It appeared in 1860.

qa.q: Burckhardt was a scholar from:
qa.e: He was Swiss, at the University of Basle.

qa.q: According to Burckhardt, a key belief of humanist culture was that:
qa.a: The individual could shape his own world, not wholly controlled by religion
qa.e: Humanism emphasised the individual and human potential.

qa.q: Which period does the European Renaissance broadly cover?
qa.e: The Renaissance is placed in the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries.

qa.q: Which source would best show changes in Renaissance art?
qa.e: Paintings and sculptures are key sources for art history.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Townspeople in Renaissance Europe often saw themselves as more 'civilised' than rural people. Reason (R): Jacob Burckhardt was a Swiss historian.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but Burckhardt's nationality does not explain townspeople's self-image, which came from growing urban culture.

qa.q: From which century did Italian towns begin to revive?
qa.e: Trade revival from the twelfth century boosted Italian ports.

qa.q: Which trade helped revive Italian ports?
qa.a: Trade between the Byzantine Empire and Islamic lands
qa.e: Byzantine-Islamic trade revived Italy's ports.

qa.q: Which two Italian cities are described as among the most vibrant city-states?
qa.e: Venice and Genoa were great trading city-states.

qa.q: What made Venice and Genoa politically different from much of Europe?
qa.a: Clergy were not dominant and there were no powerful feudal lords; merchants governed
qa.e: Merchants and bankers took part in government.

qa.q: Which family dominated Florence?
qa.e: The Medici, a wealthy banking family, dominated Florence.

qa.q: Venice in this period was a:
qa.e: Venice was a republic governed by its citizens' councils.

qa.q: Why were Italian towns the first to experience humanist ideas?
qa.a: Trade wealth, independent city-states and active citizens
qa.e: Wealth, independence and contact with other cultures fostered humanism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ideas of citizenship grew in Italian city-states. Reason (R): Rich merchants and bankers actively participated in governing these cities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; participation in government nurtured citizenship.

qa.q: Which Italian universities were early centres of legal studies?
qa.e: Padua and Bologna specialised in law from the eleventh century.

qa.q: Why was law the most popular subject in Italian universities?
qa.a: Commerce needed lawyers and notaries for agreements
qa.e: Trade depended on written contracts drafted and interpreted by legal experts.

qa.q: Francesco Petrarch lived from:
qa.e: Petrarch lived 1304-1378.

qa.q: What did Petrarch stress?
qa.a: Close reading of ancient Greek and Roman authors
qa.e: He believed antiquity was best understood through its own writers' words.

qa.q: Which subject was NOT one of the humanities taught by humanists?
qa.e: The humanities were grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy.

qa.q: The Latin word 'humanitas' was used by which Roman writer to mean culture?
qa.e: Cicero, a lawyer and essayist, used humanitas to mean culture.

qa.q: What did humanist subjects emphasise?
qa.a: Skills developed through discussion and debate
qa.e: Humanities stressed reasoning, rhetoric and debate.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The humanist programme implied that much could be learnt beyond religious teaching. Reason (R): Humanists taught only religious texts.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because humanists taught grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy.

qa.q: Which writer, a layman, wrote on religious themes and helped make Florence an intellectual centre?
qa.e: Dante (1265-1321) was a layman writing on religious themes.

qa.q: Giotto is remembered for:
qa.e: Giotto's figures were lifelike, unlike earlier stiff images.

qa.q: A 'Renaissance man' is a person who:
qa.e: Many famous figures combined several roles, such as scholar, diplomat and artist.

qa.q: The humanists believed the period after the fall of Rome was:
qa.e: They saw the Middle Ages as a dark age.

qa.q: According to humanist periodisation, the 'modern' age began in the:
qa.e: They placed the modern age from the fifteenth century.

qa.q: In the humanist view, who controlled people's minds in the Middle Ages?
qa.e: Humanists claimed the Church had full control and classical learning was lost.

qa.q: How do later historians view the humanists' periodisation?
qa.a: As debatable, since learning and achievement continued in the Middle Ages
qa.e: Historians now question the dark-age label.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Humanists called the Middle Ages a 'dark age'. Reason (R): Classical learning had disappeared completely from the world in that period.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because classical learning survived in places like Byzantium and the Arab world.

qa.q: European scholars of the fourteenth century read Plato and Aristotle largely thanks to:
qa.a: Arab translators who preserved ancient manuscripts
qa.e: Arab scholars preserved and translated Greek works.

qa.q: Ibn Sina was known in Latin as:
qa.e: Ibn Sina was Avicenna; Ibn Rushd was Averroes.

qa.q: Ibn Rushd (Averroes) was a philosopher from:
qa.e: Ibn Rushd was from Spain.

qa.q: Ibn Sina lived from:
qa.e: Ibn Sina lived 980-1037.

qa.q: Why does the title 'Almagest' carry 'al'?
qa.a: It was translated into Arabic, and 'al' is the Arabic definite article
qa.e: The Arabic article shows the work passed through Arabic translation.

qa.q: Ptolemy's Almagest was a work on:
qa.e: It was an astronomy text.

qa.q: What did Ibn Rushd try to do?
qa.a: Resolve tensions between philosophy and religious belief
qa.e: His method was adopted by Christian thinkers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Renaissance Europe owed much to Arab scholarship. Reason (R): Arab scholars preserved Greek works and contributed to mathematics, astronomy, medicine and chemistry.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; this preservation and contribution explain the debt.

qa.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
qa.e: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

qa.q: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of which chapel?
qa.e: He painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in Rome.

qa.q: Which sculptor broke new ground with lifelike statues in 1416?
qa.e: Donatello's statues of 1416 were strikingly lifelike.

qa.q: Andreas Vesalius, the pioneer of human dissection whose work began modern physiology, was a professor at:
qa.e: Vesalius taught medicine at Padua.

qa.q: Leonardo da Vinci designed a flying machine after years of:
qa.e: He studied birds closely and designed a flying machine.

qa.q: Linear perspective in painting depended mainly on:
qa.e: Geometry helped artists create the illusion of depth.

qa.q: Leonardo signed himself as:
qa.e: He called himself a disciple of experiment, showing his scientific bent.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Renaissance art became more realistic. Reason (R): Gutenberg's workshop printed the Bible in 1455.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but printing does not explain realism in art; anatomy, geometry, light and oil paints do.

qa.q: Who designed the dome of Florence's cathedral?
qa.e: Brunelleschi designed the Duomo; Michelangelo designed St Peter's dome.

qa.q: Michelangelo designed the dome of:
qa.e: He designed the dome of St Peter's Basilica.

qa.q: The 'classical' style of Renaissance architecture was a revival of:
qa.e: It revived Roman domes, arches and columns.

qa.q: Why did Rome revive as a cultural centre from 1417?
qa.a: The papacy grew stronger after the split of rival popes ended
qa.e: A stronger papacy encouraged study of Rome's past.

qa.q: A new feature of Renaissance art and architecture was that:
qa.a: Artists became known individually by name
qa.e: Individual masters became famous; patrons sought them out.

qa.q: Which element of Greek and Roman culture was revived in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries?
qa.a: Classical architecture with domes, arches and columns
qa.e: Classical texts, law, sculpture and architecture were revived.

qa.q: Which feature is typical of Islamic architecture rather than the Italian Renaissance?
qa.e: Minarets and geometric or calligraphic decoration are typical Islamic features.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Renaissance architects revived Roman styles. Reason (R): The papacy grew weaker after 1417 and discouraged the study of Rome's past.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because the papacy grew stronger after 1417 and encouraged the study of Rome's history.

qa.q: Who made the first printing press in Europe?
qa.e: Gutenberg, a German, made the first European printing press.

qa.q: In 1455, Gutenberg's workshop printed how many copies of the Bible?
qa.e: 150 copies were printed, while a monk might copy one by hand.

qa.q: In which year were 150 copies of the Bible printed in Gutenberg's workshop?
qa.e: The printing of the Bible took place in 1455.

qa.q: From whom did Europeans originally learn of printing technology?
qa.a: The Chinese, via contacts at Mongol courts
qa.e: Chinese printing became known to Europeans through Mongol-era contacts.

qa.q: What was one effect of printing?
qa.a: Ideas spread more widely and rapidly
qa.e: Cheaper books spread information faster.

qa.q: By the end of the fifteenth century, printed classical texts in Italy were mostly in:
qa.e: Most classical texts printed were in Latin.

qa.q: How did printing help humanism spread beyond Italy?
qa.a: Printed books carried humanist ideas across the Alps
qa.e: From the late fifteenth century, humanist culture spread north through print.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Students in Renaissance Europe no longer depended only on lecture notes. Reason (R): Printed books became widely available for purchase.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; available books explain the change.

qa.q: Who wrote The Prince (1513)?
qa.e: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513.

qa.q: In The Prince, Machiavelli described human beings as:
qa.a: Driven by self-interest: ungrateful, fickle and eager for gain
qa.e: He took a frank, realistic view of human nature.

qa.q: Francesco Barbaro, a Venetian humanist, defended:
qa.a: The acquisition of wealth as a virtue
qa.e: His pamphlet defended acquiring wealth.

qa.q: Lorenzo Valla's book On Pleasure criticised:
qa.e: Valla challenged the religious rejection of pleasure.

qa.q: A key feature of humanist culture was:
qa.a: A slackening of religion's control over human life
qa.e: Humanism gave more room to worldly concerns and the individual.

qa.q: Concern with good manners in Renaissance culture meant attention to:
qa.a: Speaking politely, dressing correctly and learning cultured skills
qa.e: Manners and cultivated skills became important.

qa.q: Which idea is most closely linked to the rise of individualism?
qa.a: People can shape their own lives through varied talents
qa.e: Humanists believed individuals could shape their lives.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Renaissance Italians valued material wealth, power and glory. Reason (R): They had completely abandoned religion.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false: they valued worldly success but were not necessarily irreligious.

qa.q: Cassandra Fedele was a humanist from:
qa.e: Fedele was Venetian; Isabella d'Este was of Mantua.

qa.q: Cassandra Fedele was proficient in:
qa.e: She was known for Greek and Latin and spoke at Padua.

qa.q: Cassandra Fedele lived from:
qa.e: Fedele lived 1465-1558.

qa.q: Isabella d'Este was the Marchesa of:
qa.e: She ruled Mantua when her husband was away.

qa.q: What did Cassandra Fedele criticise about the Venetian republic?
qa.a: Its limited definition of freedom that favoured men
qa.e: She criticised freedom defined in men's favour.

qa.q: In aristocratic families, women's dowries were:
qa.a: Put into family businesses, but wives had no say in running them
qa.e: Dowries funded businesses without giving wives control.

qa.q: Why did women in merchant families sometimes have a larger role than aristocratic women?
qa.a: They helped run shops and managed businesses when men were away
qa.e: Practical needs of trade gave merchant women more responsibility.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Renaissance women were fully equal to men in public life. Reason (R): Isabella d'Este ruled Mantua while her husband was absent.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because women were largely excluded from public life; R is true but exceptional.

qa.q: Which humanist from Holland criticised the Church's greed?
qa.e: Erasmus was in Holland; Thomas More in England.

qa.q: Indulgences were:
qa.a: Documents sold by the Church that apparently freed buyers from sins
qa.e: They claimed to free the buyer from all sins.

qa.q: In which year did Martin Luther launch his campaign against the Catholic Church?
qa.e: Luther's campaign began in 1517.

qa.q: Martin Luther argued that:
qa.a: A person did not need priests to establish contact with God
qa.e: He stressed direct faith in God.

qa.q: According to Luther, what alone could guide a person to the right life and to heaven?
qa.e: Luther taught that faith alone was enough.

qa.q: Into which language did Luther translate the Bible?
qa.e: Luther translated the Bible into German.

qa.q: How did Luther respond to the peasants' rebellion of 1525?
qa.a: He called on German rulers to suppress it
qa.e: Luther urged the rulers to crush the revolt.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many Christians questioned Church practices such as indulgences. Reason (R): Bibles printed in local languages let people read the scriptures for themselves.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; access to the Bible helped people question unscriptural practices.

qa.q: Who popularised Luther's ideas in Switzerland?
qa.a: Ulrich Zwingli and later Jean Calvin
qa.e: Zwingli and Calvin spread reform in Switzerland.

qa.q: Where did reformers have greater popular appeal?
qa.e: Merchants backed reformers in towns; the Catholic Church held rural areas.

qa.q: The Anabaptists argued that:
qa.a: Since God made all people equal, they need not pay taxes and could choose their own priests
qa.e: They linked salvation with ending social oppression.

qa.q: Under which English king did the Church of England separate from Rome?
qa.e: Henry VIII broke with the Pope; the monarch became head of the Church.

qa.q: The Society of Jesus was founded by:
qa.e: Ignatius Loyola founded the Jesuits.

qa.q: In which year was the Society of Jesus founded?
qa.e: It was founded in 1540.

qa.q: The Catholic Church's reform from within is called the:
qa.e: The Catholic response is known as the Counter-Reformation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Anabaptists' ideas appealed to many peasants. Reason (R): Under Henry VIII, the Church of England separated from Rome.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but events in England do not explain the Anabaptists' appeal, which came from their message against social oppression.

qa.q: What was the earlier Christian view of the universe?
qa.a: The earth was stationary at the centre
qa.e: The earth-centred view held that heavenly bodies moved around a stationary earth.

qa.q: Copernicus argued that:
qa.a: The planets, including the earth, rotate around the sun
qa.e: He proposed a heliocentric universe.

qa.q: Copernicus's book was called:
qa.e: His manuscript was De revolutionibus.

qa.q: Who showed that planets move around the sun in ellipses, not circles?
qa.e: Kepler showed elliptical orbits.

qa.q: The Copernican revolution reached its climax with:
qa.e: Newton's gravitation explained planetary motion.

qa.q: The Scientific Revolution held that knowledge should be based on:
qa.e: Knowledge, as distinct from belief, rested on observation and experiment.

qa.q: The Royal Society in London was formed in:
qa.e: The Royal Society was formed in 1662.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Copernicus hesitated to publish his theory. Reason (R): Copernicus was an atheist who mocked the Church.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because Copernicus was a devout Christian who feared the clergy's reaction.

qa.q: Which idea of Burckhardt do recent historians question?
qa.a: A sharp break between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance
qa.e: Historians stress continuity and gradual change.

qa.q: Where had classical learning been preserved before the Renaissance?
qa.a: In Byzantium and the Arab world
qa.e: Byzantine and Arab scholars kept classical learning alive.

qa.q: Which was a significant change historians accept for this period?
qa.a: A gradual separation of private and public spheres
qa.e: The private-public distinction emerged gradually.

qa.q: Which external contact did NOT shape the Renaissance?
qa.a: Direct trade with the Americas in the fourteenth century
qa.e: Europeans reached the Americas only in 1492; the others shaped the Renaissance from earlier on.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the Renaissance according to many historians today?
qa.a: A gradual cultural change linked to wider world contacts
qa.e: It was gradual and connected with the wider world.

qa.q: Humanism was being taught at Padua University by about:
qa.e: Humanism was taught at Padua around 1300.

qa.q: Which is a key feature of humanist thought?
qa.a: Emphasis on the individual and classical learning
qa.e: Humanism stressed the individual and classical studies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All historians accept Burckhardt's idea of a sudden break from the Middle Ages. Reason (R): Classical learning had been preserved in Byzantium and the Arab world.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because many historians question the sharp-break idea; R is true and is one reason they do.

qa.q: From which century did Europeans begin establishing settler colonies in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand?
qa.e: European settlement expanded from the seventeenth century.

qa.q: Which of these was a settler colony?
qa.e: Australia saw permanent large-scale European settlement.

qa.q: How did settler colonies differ from colonies in South Asia?
qa.a: Large numbers of Europeans settled permanently
qa.e: In settler colonies, Europeans came to stay in large numbers.

qa.q: What happened to native peoples in settler colonies?
qa.e: They lost land and were pushed to the margins.

qa.q: Which source gives the native peoples' own view of colonisation?
qa.e: Oral histories preserve native perspectives.

qa.q: Why do historians now value native art and testimonies?
qa.a: They add perspectives missing from settler records
qa.e: They balance a record dominated by settler voices.

qa.q: Which countries are commonly called settler colonies?
qa.a: USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand
qa.e: These had large-scale European settlement.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Native peoples in settler colonies were marginalised. Reason (R): Europeans took their lands and pushed them into remote areas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; loss of land explains their marginalisation.

qa.q: Why were the native peoples of the Americas called 'Indians'?
qa.a: Columbus believed he had reached India
qa.e: Columbus's 1492 error gave the name.

qa.q: The name 'America' comes from:
qa.e: The continents were named after Amerigo Vespucci.

qa.q: 'Aborigine' is derived from Latin words meaning:
qa.e: Ab origine means from the beginning.

qa.q: Until the twentieth century, Europeans used the word 'native' mainly for:
qa.e: It was used for colonised peoples, often implying inferiority.

qa.q: In which year did Columbus reach the Americas?
qa.e: Columbus reached the Americas in 1492.

qa.q: Which was NOT a major settler colony?
qa.e: Japan was never a European settler colony.

qa.q: Why is 'New World' considered a Eurocentric term?
qa.a: The land was new only to Europeans
qa.e: Native peoples had lived there for thousands of years.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Native Americans came to be called 'Indians'. Reason (R): Columbus thought the land he reached in 1492 was India.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; Columbus's mistake explains the name.

qa.q: The earliest inhabitants of North America came from Asia across the:
qa.e: They crossed a land-bridge across the Bering Straits more than 30,000 years ago.

qa.q: Which crop did North American native peoples cultivate?
qa.e: They grew vegetables and maize.

qa.q: Which animal did native peoples travel long distances to hunt on the plains?
qa.e: Bison, wild oxen, roamed the grassy plains.

qa.q: How did native peoples generally view land?
qa.a: As something shared for community use, not owned
qa.e: They felt no need to claim ownership of land.

qa.q: Native peoples built relationships mainly through:
qa.a: Formal alliances, friendship and gift exchanges
qa.e: Gift exchange and alliances sealed relationships.

qa.q: What did natives trade with Europeans?
qa.e: They traded furs for blankets, iron utensils, guns and alcohol.

qa.q: Why did native peoples hunt only as many bison as they needed?
qa.a: They took from the land only what they required
qa.e: This reflected their sustainable relationship with the land.

qa.q: Assertion (A): North American native peoples did not build large kingdoms or empires. Reason (R): North American natives produced huge surpluses to sell to Europe.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because they took what they needed from the land and did not seek large surpluses.

qa.q: By which standards did eighteenth-century Europeans judge a people 'civilised'?
qa.a: Literacy, organised religion and urban life
qa.e: Europeans used literacy, religion and towns as markers.

qa.q: The French philosopher Rousseau saw native peoples as:
qa.e: Rousseau idealised peoples living close to nature.

qa.q: How did native peoples tend to see the Europeans?
qa.a: As greedy for land and gold
qa.e: Natives saw Europeans as greedy.

qa.q: Why must historians read European poets' descriptions of natives carefully?
qa.a: They reflected European ideas rather than natives' own voices
qa.e: Literary portraits reveal more about the writer's world.

qa.q: Native peoples expressed their views on land mainly through:
qa.e: Speeches and petitions voiced their claims.

qa.q: What was the core contrast in attitudes to land?
qa.a: Natives saw land as shared; Europeans saw it as private property
qa.e: This difference lay at the root of conflict.

qa.q: A European visitor judges a native village 'uncivilised' because it has no written records. What is the best critique?
qa.a: It applies European standards to a society with rich oral traditions
qa.e: Oral cultures have their own complex knowledge and institutions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many Europeans considered native Americans 'uncivilised'. Reason (R): Native peoples had no knowledge of their land or climate.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because natives had deep knowledge of land and climate.

qa.q: Which law of 1830 authorised moving native peoples west of the Mississippi?
qa.e: The Indian Removal Act was passed in 1830; the Reorganisation Act came in 1934.

qa.q: Who led the Cherokees in their legal resistance?
qa.e: John Ross was the Cherokee chief.

qa.q: Which President refused to enforce the Supreme Court's ruling for the Cherokees?
qa.e: Andrew Jackson ignored the ruling.

qa.q: The Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that:
qa.a: The Cherokees were a distinct community and Georgia had no authority over them
qa.e: The Court sided with the Cherokees, but its ruling was ignored.

qa.q: About how many Cherokees were forced to leave on the Trail of Tears?
qa.e: About 15,000 were driven out.

qa.q: If about one-quarter of 15,000 Cherokees died on the Trail of Tears, roughly how many died?
'Reservations' in the USA were:
qa.a: Small areas of land to which natives were confined
qa.e: Natives were pushed into reservations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Native peoples in the USA sold their land at fair prices in every treaty. Reason (R): The Indian Removal Act was passed in 1830.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, because treaties often paid very low prices and involved deception; R is true.

qa.q: What was the 'gold rush'?
qa.a: Thousands rushing to California hoping to find gold
qa.e: Gold in California drew thousands seeking fortune.

qa.q: Which workers were recruited in large numbers to build the US railways?
qa.e: Chinese and Irish workers built much of the railway.

qa.q: Canada's transcontinental railway was completed in:
qa.e: It was completed in 1885.

qa.q: Which industries grew with the railways?
qa.e: Railways and large-scale farming created new industries.

qa.q: Cotton plantations in the southern USA were worked mainly by:
qa.e: Enslaved Africans worked the plantations.

qa.q: The American Civil War took place in:
qa.e: The Civil War lasted from 1861 to 1865.

qa.q: What was a major result of the Civil War?
qa.e: Slavery was abolished.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Industrial expansion in the nineteenth century worsened the condition of native peoples. Reason (R): The American Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the Civil War, fought over slavery, does not explain harm to natives; railways, farms and settlers on their land do.

qa.q: In which year were native peoples in the USA recognised as citizens?
qa.e: Natives became US citizens in 1924.

qa.q: The Indian Reorganisation Act of 1934 gave natives in reservations the right to:
qa.e: It allowed them to buy land and take loans.

qa.q: The Declaration of Indian Rights (1954) was prepared by:
qa.a: The National Congress of American Indians
qa.e: The National Congress of American Indians drafted it.

qa.q: On what condition did the Declaration of Indian Rights accept US citizenship?
qa.a: That reservations would not be taken away and traditions not interfered with
qa.e: Natives accepted citizenship while protecting land and traditions.

qa.q: Canada's Constitution Act of 1982:
qa.a: Accepted existing aboriginal rights and treaty rights
qa.e: It recognised existing aboriginal and treaty rights.

qa.q: Why did the late-nineteenth-century attempt to break reservations into individual plots harm natives?
qa.a: It undermined community ownership and their way of life
qa.e: Breaking communal land weakened native communities.

qa.q: The democratic rights in the original US Constitution:
qa.a: Did not at first extend to natives
qa.e: Natives were excluded from these rights at first.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Native rights in North America were recognised only slowly. Reason (R): Natives became US citizens only in 1924, and Canada recognised aboriginal rights only in 1982.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these late dates show the slow pace.

qa.q: Who reached Botany Bay in 1770?
qa.e: Captain Cook reached Botany Bay and named New South Wales.

qa.q: British settlement in Australia began in 1788 with the arrival of:
qa.e: The first settlers were convicts.

qa.q: By the late eighteenth century, how many native communities lived in Australia, each with its own language?
qa.e: There were 350-750 communities.

qa.q: What does 'terra nullius' mean?
qa.a: Empty land belonging to no one
qa.e: It treated Australia as empty, ignoring its native peoples.

qa.q: How did British settlement in Australia spread?
qa.a: By seizing land and driving natives away
qa.e: Land was taken by force; natives were killed or displaced.

qa.q: Why did many Aborigines die after Europeans arrived?
qa.a: Violence and diseases to which they had no immunity
qa.e: Violence and disease devastated native communities.

qa.q: The Torres Strait Islanders are native people of Australia's:
qa.e: They live in the north, between Australia and New Guinea.

qa.q: Assertion (A): British settlers took Aboriginal land in Australia. Reason (R): The British signed treaties buying land fairly from every Aboriginal community.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because under terra nullius land was taken without treaties.

qa.q: Which activity was central to Australia's early colonial economy?
qa.e: Large-scale sheep farming produced wool.

qa.q: The White Australia policy:
qa.e: It favoured European immigrants and restricted Asians.

qa.q: Which city was built as Australia's capital?
qa.e: Canberra was built as the capital.

qa.q: In what way did Australian displacement differ from that in North America?
qa.a: Australia took land without treaties, under terra nullius
qa.e: Terra nullius meant no treaties in Australia.

qa.q: Which was common to both North America and Australia?
qa.a: Natives lost land and suffered from European diseases
qa.e: Land loss and disease affected natives in both.

qa.q: Why did economic growth in Australia harm natives?
qa.a: Sheep runs, farms and mines spread over native land
qa.e: Expansion of farming and mining took native land.

qa.q: A historian wants to compare displacement in the USA and Australia. Which pair of terms is most useful?
qa.e: Treaties (North America) and terra nullius (Australia) capture the key difference.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Asian immigrants faced restrictions in Australia. Reason (R): Canberra was built as Australia's capital.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but building Canberra does not explain immigration restrictions; the White Australia policy does.

qa.q: Who gave the 1968 lecture 'The Great Australian Silence'?
qa.e: The anthropologist W.E.H. Stanner gave the lecture.

qa.q: What did 'The Great Australian Silence' refer to?
qa.e: Histories had ignored the Aborigines.

qa.q: In which year was Stanner's lecture given?
qa.e: Stanner spoke in 1968.

qa.q: From which year did multiculturalism become official policy in Australia?
qa.e: Multiculturalism became policy from 1974.

qa.q: Multiculturalism in Australia meant:
qa.a: Equal respect for native cultures and immigrant cultures
qa.e: It respected native and immigrant cultures equally.

qa.q: Which injustice against Aboriginal people was later officially acknowledged?
qa.a: The forcible separation of children from their families
qa.e: Removing children from families was acknowledged; the Trail of Tears was in the USA.

qa.q: How did older history textbooks often present native peoples?
qa.a: As a footnote or not at all
qa.e: Natives were marginalised in textbooks too.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Australian histories always gave full attention to Aboriginal people. Reason (R): W.E.H. Stanner spoke of 'The Great Australian Silence' in 1968.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true, and Stanner's lecture criticised precisely this silence.

qa.q: Which are the four largest islands of Japan?
qa.e: These four make up most of Japan.

qa.q: About what proportion of Japan's land is mountainous?
qa.e: Over three-quarters is mountainous, so people live on the plains.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of China's three major river systems?
qa.e: The Ganga is in India; China's are the Yellow, Yangtze and Pearl.

qa.q: Which is the dominant ethnic group in China?
qa.e: The Han are the majority; others include the Uighur, Hui, Manchu and Tibetans.

qa.q: Which statement best contrasts Japan's and China's paths to modernisation?
qa.a: Japan industrialised under a strong state; China went through revolutions to a communist state
qa.e: Their paths diverged sharply.

qa.q: Japan's location in an earthquake zone and mostly mountainous land meant that:
qa.a: Most people lived on the plains
qa.e: Settlement concentrated on the limited plains.

qa.q: Which source would help a historian study Meiji-era ideas?
qa.a: Writings of Japanese intellectuals and newspapers
qa.e: Contemporary writings reveal debates of the period.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Japan's modernisation is often called state-led. Reason (R): The government actively drove industrialisation, education and military reform.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; government direction explains the label.

qa.q: The Tokugawa family held the position of shogun from:
qa.e: The Tokugawa shogunate lasted 1603-1867.

qa.q: Under the Tokugawa, where did the shogun rule from?
qa.e: The shogun ruled from Edo; the emperor lived in Kyoto.

qa.q: Lords of domains in Tokugawa Japan were called:
qa.e: Daimyo ruled over 250 domains.

qa.q: Who were the samurai?
qa.a: The warrior class who formed the ruling elite
qa.e: Samurai served the shogun and daimyo.

qa.q: Which late-sixteenth-century change ensured peace and order?
qa.a: Peasants were disarmed; only samurai carried swords
qa.e: Disarming peasants concentrated arms in the samurai class.

qa.q: Why were land surveys important in Tokugawa Japan?
qa.a: They identified taxpayers and graded land for a stable revenue base
qa.e: Surveys underpinned a stable tax system.

qa.q: Which feature shows a developing commercial economy in Tokugawa Japan?
qa.e: The rice stock market and money use show commercial growth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): By the mid-seventeenth century, Edo was the most populous city in the world. Reason (R): Rich merchants patronised theatre such as Kabuki.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but merchant patronage of theatre does not explain Edo's size, which owed much to daimyo and their retinues living there and to commerce.

qa.q: Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in Japan in:
qa.e: Perry arrived in 1853.

qa.q: Perry came from which country?
qa.e: Perry was an American naval officer.

qa.q: In which year did the Meiji Restoration take place?
qa.e: The emperor was restored in 1868.

qa.q: After the Meiji Restoration, Edo was renamed:
qa.e: Edo became Tokyo, the eastern capital.

qa.q: The Meiji slogan 'fukoku kyohei' meant:
qa.e: It meant a rich country and a strong army.

qa.q: The Meiji Constitution of 1889 was modelled on the constitution of:
qa.e: It followed the German model.

qa.q: What replaced the daimyo domains under the Meiji government?
qa.e: Domains were abolished and prefectures created.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Meiji schools stressed loyalty to the nation. Reason (R): Meiji schooling was open only to boys.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because schooling was compulsory for boys and girls.

qa.q: Japan's first railway line, built in 1870-72, linked Tokyo with:
qa.e: The line ran between Tokyo and the port of Yokohama.

qa.q: The main source of funds for Meiji modernisation was:
qa.e: Agricultural taxes financed modernisation.

qa.q: Zaibatsu were:
qa.a: Big business organisations controlled by particular families
qa.e: Zaibatsu were family-controlled conglomerates.

qa.q: Which companies were helped by subsidies to become major shipbuilders?
qa.e: Mitsubishi and Sumitomo became Japanese industrial giants.

qa.q: To where did the Meiji government encourage migration to ease population pressure?
qa.a: Hokkaido, then Hawaii, Brazil and Japan's colonies
qa.e: Migration went to Hokkaido, then overseas.

qa.q: Tanaka Shozo is remembered for leading a protest in 1897 against:
qa.a: Pollution from the Ashio copper mine
qa.e: It was Japan's first popular movement against industrial pollution.

qa.q: A large share of Japan's modern factory workers were:
qa.e: More than half the workers in modern factories were women.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Industrialisation in Meiji Japan damaged the environment. Reason (R): Mines and factories polluted rivers and land, as at the Ashio copper mine.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the Ashio case shows the damage.

qa.q: Which Meiji intellectual argued that Japan must 'expel Asia'?
qa.e: Fukuzawa wanted Japan to shed its Asian traits and become Western.

qa.q: Ueki Emori was a leader of the:
qa.a: Popular Rights (Freedom and People's Rights) movement
qa.e: He demanded constitutional government and admired natural rights.

qa.q: Miyake Setsurei argued that:
qa.a: Each nation should develop its special talents for world civilisation
qa.e: He stressed national character within a world civilisation.

qa.q: Japan fought a war with Russia in:
qa.e: The Russo-Japanese War was 1904-05; the war with China was 1894-95.

qa.q: Japan made Korea its colony in:
qa.e: Korea was colonised in 1910; Taiwan was acquired in 1895.

qa.q: To whom were Japan's armed forces directly answerable?
qa.e: The armed forces answered directly to the emperor, limiting civilian control.

qa.q: Which statement about the Meiji Constitution is correct?
qa.a: It created a Diet with limited powers and limited franchise
qa.e: Franchise and the Diet's powers were limited.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The military became very powerful in modern Japan. Reason (R): Japan's armed forces were controlled by the elected Diet.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because the armed forces answered directly to the emperor.

qa.q: Which family form became an ideal for Japan's new urban middle class?
qa.e: The nuclear family with husband and wife at the centre became the ideal.
